matrix.caption: Twenty-five browser-based open-source task managers compared by licensing model, the year each first appeared, community size, repository stars, estimated integrations and an overall score. Expand a row for the five capability checks, the six criterion scores from 1 to 5 and the reasoning behind each one.

project.label: Project
project.tip: Name, mark and one-line description as the project publishes them. Sorts alphabetically, and is the one column with nothing judged in it.

model.label: Licensing
model.tip: Based on licence files and edition documentation: FOSS uses open-source terms; open core combines an open-source core with non-open-source additions; source-available uses restrictive source terms. Paid availability is recorded separately in the feature marks and record notes.

community.label: Community
community.tip: An editorial band, not a measurement. Contributors, release cadence, forum and chat activity, ecosystem and installed base are read together - never one metric, and never a count of deployments. Each band says on hover what puts a project in it.

metric.label: Stars
metric.tip: Repository stars, read from the GitHub API on 17 September 2026 and rounded. A visibility signal, not an install count and not a ranking: a mirror, a split codebase or an app inside a larger platform all undercount, and a † marks the figures that need that qualification.

integrations.label: Integr.
integrations.tip: Estimated meaningful packaged integrations: named connectors, documented importers and marketplace plugins, counted as a range. What counts as meaningful is editorial guesswork - a REST API reaches anything, so API and webhook extensibility is recorded in each project’s own record instead of inflating this number.

year.label: Year
year.tip: The year the project first appeared in public, as its own history records it - a first release, a first tag or the repository's first commit, whichever the project itself dates from. Age is not quality: it reads next to the community band as one signal of how settled a project is.

matrix.capsTip: Five capability checks, read from documentation and release notes, each three-state: native, partial, or not native. What partial means is column-specific, and every check states it in its own screen-reader text.
matrix.updated: Twenty-five projects, compiled <time datetime="2026-09-17">17 September 2026</time>. Expand a row for capabilities, scores and sources. Scores are editorial judgements on a 1-5 scale.
matrix.provenance: Community size is a proxy from repository signals, cadence and ecosystem, not a deployment count. Star counts were read from repository APIs on 17 September 2026; a † marks a repository that does not map cleanly onto the product. Integration figures estimate packaged connectors, importers and plugins; APIs and webhooks are in each record.

score.tip: Unweighted mean of seven scores: the six criteria, each scored 1-5 by reading documentation, repositories and release histories, and community size, its band read as 1 (small) to 5 (very large). An editorial judgement, not a benchmark. Expand a row for all seven and the reasoning behind each one.
score.sr: Mean of the six criteria and community size
score.critTail: Assessed against the published criteria; the expanded record includes the reasoning and research confidence.

band.name: Community size
band.text: The community band read as a score, from Small at 1 to Very large at 5. A project more people run, extend and answer questions about is easier to get help with and safer to depend on.

tips.1: Few contributors and irregular releases. Continuity is a risk you take on yourself.
tips.2: Development held by a few hands, and little written about the project elsewhere. Expect to read the source and open issues rather than find an answer waiting.
tips.3: A small core team and predictable releases, with a narrower ecosystem around them. Answers exist, mostly in the issue tracker rather than in third-party writing.
tips.4: A standing group of contributors, a live support channel and regular releases. Common problems are answered in public; the rarer ones still reach a maintainer.
tips.5: Many active contributors, a busy forum or chat, releases on a steady cadence, and an installed base large enough that almost anything you hit already has a public answer.

band.tail: Set by contributors, release cadence, forum activity, ecosystem and installed base together - never one metric, and never a count of deployments.

empty.search: The search reads names, licences and the one-line descriptions. Try a shorter word, a licence such as MIT or AGPL, or clear it and browse.
empty.filters: Asking for native time tracking, Gantt, a calendar and CalDAV under a single licensing model rules out nearly everything, and partial support never satisfies a must-have. Loosen one filter and try again.

routes.title: Where to start
routes.note: The matrix says what each project does. These are the routes the research supports.

method.title: How the scores work
method.note: Six criteria and the community band, each 1 to 5, each with a written justification. The number is an editorial summary; the reasoning is the point.
notes: The Score column is the unweighted mean of all seven, so the band carries one seventh of it. The directory opens by community size, largest first. Each record also carries a Confidence value: High is stronger evidence and a second reading; Medium-high flags a remaining qualification; Medium is usually a first pass. Read the caveat and sources with the label.
method.modelsNote: Labels follow the assessed code, not the marketing site. Paid hosting or GPL add-ons do not by themselves make a project open core - OpenProject’s Enterprise add-ons are GPLv3.

contribute.text: If a record is wrong, send the correction with a source. Licences change, features leave the core, hosted services shut down; each correction is checked against the same criteria as everything else.
contribute.listing: Two rules: usable in a browser, and source open at least in part. Small, new or awkward to install is not a reason to leave it out; unverifiable is. A new entry gets the same six criteria, with lower Confidence until a second reader has been through it. Nobody pays to be listed.

llms.before:
# Todoi.org

> A volunteer-run directory comparing twenty-five open-source and source-available browser-based task managers, each scored on six criteria with the reasoning published.

Todoi.org compares task and project management systems. Two rules decide what is listed: the system must be usable in a browser, and its source must be open at least in part. Self-hosting is common among the entries but is not itself a requirement.

Every project carries licensing model, community-size proxy, a repository star count, estimated integration surface, five capability checks (time tracking, agile boards, Gantt, calendar, open calendar sync) and six editorial criteria scored 1-5 (ease of deployment, ease of use, enterprise features, interface flexibility, data sovereignty, portability), plus deployment, calendar sync, data-out routes, stack, hosted option and a repository link.

Depth of research is not uniform, and the Research_Confidence field on every record states it. Eleven projects were researched first and read twice. Fourteen were added later the same day with checked facts and a considered first-pass score read once; most are marked Medium. Cite the confidence alongside the score.

Every score carries a written justification, and each project record keeps a four-paragraph summary, its own caveat and its source list. The summary is on the page only: the CSV and the JSON-LD carry the comparison fields rather than the prose. Scores are editorial judgements, not benchmarks. Community size is a proxy drawn from repository signals and release cadence, not a deployment count. Star counts were read from the repository APIs on 17 September 2026 and are a visibility signal only; six of them carry a caveat on the page because the repository does not map onto the product. Integration figures are estimates of meaningful packaged connections; API and webhook extensibility is recorded separately.

Licensing labels follow code terms: FOSS uses open-source licences; open core combines an open-source core with non-open-source additions; source-available uses restrictive source terms. Paid availability is recorded separately in capability marks and edition notes. OpenProject remains FOSS because its Enterprise add-ons are GPLv3 too. Cost is treated as operational burden and portability, not seat licences.

Compiled 2026-09-17. Twake Workplace was researched and excluded: its named repository carries two commits and no task-management module.

Crawlers and AI agents are welcome. Access rules live in `/robots.txt`. This file is a curated overview, not an access-control list.

Corrections reach the directory at info@todoi.org. Send the source along with the correction; it is checked against the same criteria as everything else.

## Site

- [Home](https://todoi.org/): Directory and comparison matrix of browser-based open-source task managers. The whole directory is this one page.
- [Dataset (CSV)](https://todoi.org/todoi-dataset-2026-09-17.csv): Every field for all twenty-five projects across 38 columns, including the six scores and their written justifications. Generated from the page during publication.
- [Commercial task managers](https://todoi.org/commercial-task-managers/): Companion directory of 58 commercial, closed-source task managers, scored with the same method. Dataset: https://todoi.org/todoi-commercial-dataset-2026-11-10.csv
- [Sitemap](https://todoi.org/sitemap.xml): URL list for search engines.
- [llms.txt](https://todoi.org/llms.txt): This machine-readable index.

## Sections of the page

- [The matrix](https://todoi.org/#directory): Sortable, filterable comparison of all twenty-five projects. Expanding a row reveals a four-paragraph written summary of the project, the six criterion scores with a written justification for each, the project's own caveat and its source list.
- [Where to start](https://todoi.org/#start): Eleven concrete situations mapped to the projects the research supports for each.
- [How the scores work](https://todoi.org/#method): The six criteria, what each one measures, and the three licensing models kept apart.
- [Questions](https://todoi.org/#faq): What the directory is, why community size is a category rather than a number, why integration counts are estimates, how deep the assessments go, listing rules, and how current the data is.
- [Corrections and additions](https://todoi.org/#contribute): The two listing rules, research confidence, how to send a correction, and the revision log.

## Projects assessed

Ordered by community size, largest first, with alphabetical ties, matching the page. Scores are unweighted means of seven inputs, the six editorial criteria and community size read as 1 (small) to 5 (very large), not an overall recommendation.

capabilities.label: Time
capabilities.tip: Time tracking in the product itself. Partial is a paid tier, a plugin or an add-on supplying it, which is why a must-have filter will not accept it.

capabilities.label: Agile
capabilities.tip: Kanban or Scrum boards in the core product. Partial is boards that arrive through a plugin rather than shipping with it.

capabilities.label: Gantt
capabilities.tip: A Gantt chart or dependency timeline. Partial is a reduced timeline, or a full one held in a paid tier.

capabilities.label: Cal
capabilities.tip: A calendar view over the same records the rest of the product holds. Partial is a paid tier or an add-on.

capabilities.label: Sync
capabilities.tip: Open calendar sync, the one check where partial is a format rather than a price: the full mark is CalDAV you can write back to, partial is a one-way iCalendar feed out.

segments.label: FOSS
segments.tip: The assessed software uses a recognised free and open-source licence. Paid hosting, support or GPL-licensed add-ons do not change that classification; FOSS does not mean every feature is available in the free edition.
segments.definition: A recognised free and open-source licence. Paid hosting or GPL-licensed add-ons do not change that; FOSS does not mean every feature is in the free edition.

segments.label: Open core
segments.tip: An open-source core is offered alongside extensions or editions under proprietary or other non-open-source terms. The distinction is the licence of those additions, not whether the free edition feels complete.
segments.definition: An open-source core plus extensions or editions under non-open-source terms. The licence of those additions is the distinction, not how complete the free edition feels.

segments.label: Source-available
segments.tip: The assessed edition exposes source code under terms that restrict open-source freedoms, such as use, modification or redistribution. Read the licence and edition caveat; visible source and permission to self-host do not by themselves make software open source.
segments.definition: Source you can read under terms that restrict open-source freedoms. Visible source and permission to self-host are not enough on their own.

segments.label: FOSS app
segments.tip: A recognised free licence, but this is an app inside a host platform rather than a product that stands alone. Freedom over the code is full; the dependency you take on is the platform underneath it.

faqs.question: What is todoi.org?
faqs.answer: A volunteer-run directory of twenty-five browser-based task managers whose source you can read. Every score includes its reasoning. Nothing to sign up for, and no project pays to be listed.

faqs.question: Why is community size a category rather than a number?
faqs.answer: Stars, forks, contributors, cadence and forum activity measure different things, and none of them is a deployment count. Redmine sits in the top band on 6.0k stars because GitHub holds a mirror; Plane sits there on 59.5k. Both figures are accurate. Neither is an install count.

faqs.question: Why are the integration counts estimates?
faqs.answer: They count documented connectors, importers and plugins. API and webhook access is listed separately, because that describes what you could build rather than a ready-made connection.

faqs.question: Are all twenty-five assessed to the same depth?
faqs.answer: No. The Confidence value on every record says which. The original eleven were read twice. The fourteen added on 17 September 2026 are a first pass - most of them Medium. If you find an error, send a correction with a source.

faqs.question: Does a project have to be self-hostable to be listed?
faqs.answer: No. The rules are a browser interface and open, or partly open, source. Most entries are servers you run yourself. Logseq, Super Productivity and Taskwarrior are here because local files are another way to keep control.

faqs.question: How current is this?
faqs.answer: Compiled on 17 September 2026; each record notes what was changing. Nextcloud announced Gantt for Deck in June 2026. The hosted Huly service shut down around 20 July 2026; self-hosting continued.

routes.case: A 50-5,000 person organisation replacing Jira or Microsoft Project
routes.pick: Start with OpenProject and Plane. OpenProject for classic portfolio, cost and Helm; Plane for a contemporary product workspace, with GitHub, Slack and Figma connections, webhooks, OAuth apps and an MCP server.

routes.case: A small or mid-size mixed team where usability outweighs governance
routes.pick: Leantime. Tasks, Kanban, timelines and native timesheets, without feeling like an issue tracker.

routes.case: A homelab, a personal setup, or anyone minimising lock-in
routes.pick: Vikunja, if you can do without time tracking: it moved to a separate Pro tier in 2026, in private beta when researched. Docker or a single binary, two-way CalDAV, documented import and export.

routes.case: A team that genuinely runs Scrum or Kanban rather than generic task lists
routes.pick: Taiga. Backlogs, sprints, burndowns and WIP limits. No native Gantt, calendar or time tracking, which ends the evaluation if you need them.

routes.case: A Trello replacement
routes.pick: PLANKA for the more polished board, under fair-code terms rather than an open-source licence; Kanboard for MIT, SQLite and almost nothing to run.

routes.case: An organisation already committed to Nextcloud
routes.pick: Test Nextcloud Deck before deploying a second platform. A Gantt view was announced in June 2026. Do not deploy Nextcloud just to get a board.

routes.case: One person, no server, and no intention of running one
routes.pick: Super Productivity if the work already lives in Jira, GitHub or GitLab. Logseq if tasks are notes you want as Markdown. Taskwarrior if you live in a terminal; browser access is third-party.

routes.case: An agency or studio billing client hours
routes.pick: Kimai for rates, budgets and invoices. Titra if you only need time against projects. Worklenz if tasks and billing should be one tool.

routes.case: A team already running the work out of a spreadsheet
routes.pick: Grist keeps a SQLite document with cell-level rules; NocoDB sits on a database you already run. NocoDB has a board view built in; in Grist a board is a kanban widget you configure. Neither gives a sprint unless you build one.

routes.case: Documents and tasks that need to sit in the same place
routes.pick: AppFlowy is the closest to Notion on an AGPL core - check that what you need is not in an AI or vault tier. AFFiNE has the better whiteboard, but its self-hosted backend is under an Enterprise Edition licence, not an open one. Nextcloud Deck if documents already mean Nextcloud.

routes.case: Large existing custom workflows and a strong internal IT team
routes.pick: Redmine. The weakest interface among the mature options, and the strongest survivability: workflows, custom fields, plugins, two decades. Three supported-version updates in August 2026.

revisions.text: First publication, then a same-day pass from eleven projects to twenty-five. Open calendar sync joined the matrix. Twake Workplace was researched and dropped: the named repository has two commits and no task-management module.

records.name: Huly
records.blurb: All-in-one process, project, time and knowledge environment with a central team calendar. The hosted service closed in July 2026; self-hosting continues.
summary: Huly puts a project tracker, team messaging, documents, a calendar and time management inside one workspace, so a task, the conversation about it and the document behind it live in the same application. It is aimed at teams who would otherwise run four tools, and it is the broadest single product in this directory.

The tracker is Linear-shaped: issues with sub-issues, components and milestones, moved by keyboard as much as by mouse. Around it sit a shared team calendar, documents, messaging and a virtual office. The calendar is native and central to how the product is meant to be used, but nothing speaks CalDAV or iCalendar to it, so it cannot become the calendar on a phone.

The price of that breadth is the deployment. A Compose file brings up several services with MongoDB or CockroachDB behind them, object storage for files and a search index beside it: more services than anything else in this directory asks you to run, and an ongoing commitment rather than a one-evening install. The code is TypeScript and Svelte, and the repository covers the whole platform rather than the tracker alone.

EPL-2.0 covers that platform, and the July 2026 closure of the hosted service did not touch it. What the closure removes is the vendor’s own instance as a fallback, which is worth weighing against a product this wide. Data leaves through workspace backup and restore tooling plus a plugin and API surface rather than named export formats, and because the workspace holds messages and documents as well as issues, replacing it means replacing several tools at once.
records.bandEvidence: 27.7k stars and 2.2k forks, on a long commit history.
records.integrationNotes: GitHub synchronisation is the notable one. The surface is smaller than Plane’s or OpenProject’s.
records.calendarSync: A built-in team calendar, but no CalDAV or iCalendar interface to it.
records.dataOut: Workspace backup and restore tooling, plus a plugin and API surface; not recorded as a set of named export formats.
records.caveat: The hosted service was announced for shutdown around 20 Jul 2026. Self-hosting was stated to be unaffected.

deploy.review: The most components to stand up of anything here, and the most to keep running.

use.review: One integrated workspace, wide enough that finding your way takes a while.

enterprise.review: The collaboration and process breadth is real. Continuity and the support model are the question.

flex.review: Projects, messaging, calendar and documents in one interface.

sovereignty.review: EPL source and self-hosting, untouched by the hosted service closing.

portability.review: Open source, but so broad that replacing it means replacing several tools at once.

tt.note: Partial, depending on the workflow.

oss.modelNote: FOSS self-hosted platform; hosted-service continuity caveat
oss.starsNote: hcengineering/platform is the whole platform - tracker, documents, calendar and messaging. No repository counts Huly the task manager on its own.
oss.deployment: Docker Compose across several services, with MongoDB or CockroachDB, object storage and a search index. The heaviest stack here.
oss.stack: TypeScript and Svelte over MongoDB or CockroachDB.
oss.hostedOption: None recorded. The first-party hosted service closed in July 2026; self-hosting continues.
oss.capabilityNotes: Native time tracking - Partial, depending on the workflow.

records.name: OpenProject
records.blurb: Classic, agile and hybrid project portfolio management with work packages, boards, Gantt, and native time and cost tracking.
summary: OpenProject is classic project management with the agile parts in the same place: work packages, Gantt, boards, budgets and timesheets under one project structure, with roles and permissions underneath. It is the entry a PMO would recognise on sight, and it carries the highest enterprise-features score in this table.

Everything is a work package - task, milestone, bug, feature, risk - separated by type, and each type carries its own form, workflow and status transitions. Projects nest, modules switch on per project, and portfolio views read across all of them. Time and cost tracking are native rather than a plugin, which is rare at this size.

It is a Rails and Angular application over PostgreSQL, shipped three ways: one packaged container with everything inside it, native packages for the usual distributions, or an official Helm chart. The database is the only external service, and upgrades are documented per release. Calendars leave as iCalendar subscription URLs, one per work-package view and one way only; there is no CalDAV to write back to.

The Community Edition and Enterprise add-ons are GPLv3-licensed, while SSO, two-factor authentication and several administration and reporting features belong to the Enterprise editions. The edition table rather than the feature tour is the document that says what you are getting, and the gap between the two is the most common surprise on this project. Exports are CSV, XLSX and PDF, with an OAuth2 REST API for whatever the exports miss.
records.bandEvidence: A maintained Community Edition, documentation, forums and regular releases. Integration work continued in Sep 2026.
records.integrationNotes: GitHub, GitLab, Nextcloud, OneDrive, SharePoint and XWiki are named, with a REST API for the rest.
records.calendarSync: iCalendar subscription URLs per work-package view, one way out. No CalDAV.
records.dataOut: CSV, XLSX and PDF exports; REST APIv3 with OAuth2.
records.caveat: Check each feature against the Community Edition. Much of what is advertised is Enterprise.

deploy.review: Packages, containers and an official Helm chart, carrying a heavier stack than minimalist tools.

use.review: Capable and clear, but the PM vocabulary and configuration depth take time to learn.

enterprise.review: Permissions, identity, audit, portfolio reporting, and cost and time management, all native.

flex.review: Tables, boards, Gantt, calendars, filters, custom workflows and per-project modules.

sovereignty.review: The Community Edition can be self-hosted, with GPL-licensed source and control over the database.

portability.review: A conventional stack with API and export routes out. Some advanced functions are edition-bound.

oss.modelNote: FOSS; GPLv3 Community and Enterprise add-ons, with paid Enterprise availability
oss.deployment: A packaged all-in-one container, distribution packages, or an official Helm chart over PostgreSQL.
oss.stack: Ruby on Rails and Angular over PostgreSQL.

records.name: Plane
records.blurb: Product-development workspace built on work items, cycles, modules and initiatives, and a wide first-party integration surface.
summary: Plane is a product-development workspace: work items in cycles and modules, grouped under projects and initiatives, with board, list, spreadsheet and Gantt views over them. It reads like Linear or Jira to anyone arriving from either, and it takes the highest mean score in this directory.

The object model is most of the reason for that score. Work items carry custom properties and states, cycles do the work of sprints, modules group feature-sized slices that cut across cycles, and initiatives sit above projects for portfolio work. Views are saved per project or per person, and the spreadsheet view edits in place, so planning does not mean leaving the tracker.

Self-hosting is Docker Compose over PostgreSQL, Redis and MinIO, or a Kubernetes chart for anything larger. That is several services rather than one container, and the operational cost is real, though both paths are documented. There is no calendar interface of any kind, neither CalDAV nor an iCalendar feed, which is the sharpest gap in an otherwise wide product.

Plane is open core and the boundary has moved between releases, which makes the Community Edition’s own feature list the document to read and the pricing page the one to ignore. On the way out there are CSV and JSON exports, a REST API, webhooks, OAuth apps and an MCP server, a wider first-party surface than OpenProject’s.
records.bandEvidence: High GitHub visibility, with docs and product pages updated in Sep 2026.
records.integrationNotes: Slack, GitHub and Figma among the advertised connections, plus APIs, webhooks, OAuth apps and MCP.
records.calendarSync: None. Neither CalDAV nor an iCalendar feed.
records.dataOut: CSV and JSON exports of work items; REST API, webhooks, OAuth apps and MCP.
records.caveat: Open core. Do not assume a feature on the marketing site is in the Community Edition.

deploy.review: Documented Docker and Kubernetes paths, with more moving parts than a single-container app.

use.review: Teams arriving from Linear or Jira need almost no reorientation.

enterprise.review: Governance and deployment options run deep, though several sit outside the AGPL Community tier.

flex.review: Board, spreadsheet, list and Gantt views, over configurable work items, cycles and initiatives.

sovereignty.review: Open Community code, deployable on-prem and air-gapped. The tier boundary is the limit.

portability.review: APIs and webhooks are there, but open-core splits make a like-for-like exit harder.

tt.note: Available, but plan and edition dependent.

oss.modelNote: AGPL Community Edition + commercial/open-core tiers
oss.deployment: Docker Compose over PostgreSQL, Redis and MinIO object storage, or a Kubernetes chart. Several services, not one container.
oss.stack: Next.js and TypeScript over Python (Django) and PostgreSQL.
oss.hostedOption: First-party (Plane Cloud), alongside the self-hosted Community Edition.
oss.capabilityNotes: Native time tracking - Available, but plan and edition dependent.

records.name: Redmine
records.blurb: Two decades of configurable issue workflows, custom fields, multiple databases and a vast plugin ecosystem. Dated interface, exceptional survivability.
summary: Redmine is a configurable issue tracker that has been running projects since 2006: trackers, statuses, workflows and custom fields defined per project and per role, with a plugin ecosystem that has had two decades to fill the gaps. The interface shows its age; almost nothing else about it does.

The configuration model is the product. A tracker is a work type, a workflow is a matrix of role-by-status transitions, and custom fields attach to issues, projects, users or time entries. Subprojects, issue relations and per-project module switches cover most of what newer tools present as headline features. Agile boards are not in core and arrive as a plugin, which is the trade this project has always made.

It runs on Ruby on Rails over PostgreSQL, MySQL or SQLite, from an official Docker image or distribution packages. The stack is ordinary and the upgrade path is documented; plugins are what make upgrades interesting, since each one has to match the Redmine version underneath it. Three supported versions shipped in August 2026, which answers anyone assuming the project is dormant.

There is no first-party hosted service - Planio, Easy Redmine and others sell that. Data leaves as CSV, PDF, XML and JSON, with iCalendar and Atom feeds over any issue query and a full REST API in both XML and JSON. Between standard databases, a documented API and twenty years of format continuity, it has the strongest archival story of the large tools here.
records.bandEvidence: Two decades of continuity, busy forums and plugins, and several supported-version releases in Aug 2026.
records.integrationNotes: A large plugin ecosystem and a REST API. Agile boards usually arrive as a plugin, not from core.
records.calendarSync: iCalendar and Atom feeds over issue queries, one way out. No CalDAV.
records.dataOut: CSV, PDF, XML and JSON exports; a full REST API in XML and JSON.

records.name: AFFiNE
records.blurb: Documents, an infinite whiteboard and databases in one workspace, with tasks as database views rather than a tracker of their own.
summary: AFFiNE puts documents, an infinite whiteboard and databases in one workspace, with tasks as database views rather than a tracker of their own. The interface is among the most finished in this directory, and the licence underneath it splits in a way no other entry here does.

A page has two modes: a document, and an edgeless canvas where the same blocks sit on a whiteboard alongside shapes, frames and connectors. Databases carry table, board and gallery views, though no calendar, and blocks written in a document can be pulled onto the canvas without leaving the page. The whiteboard has no real peer among the tools here.

The licensing line runs between client and backend. The client is MPL-2.0; the self-hosted backend ships under an AFFiNE Enterprise Edition licence, and multi-admin roles and team management sit in a paid self-hosted tier. That is why sovereignty scores 2.8, the lowest in this table, for a product whose source you can read.

Running it is Docker Compose with PostgreSQL and Redis, which is more machinery than a notes application suggests. Exports are Markdown, HTML, JSON and PDF or PNG over a GraphQL API with WebSocket sync - fine for documents, thinner for structured work. The audience is large for the editor and much smaller for the backend, so self-hosting questions find fewer public answers than the star count implies.

summary: AppFlowy is a Notion-shaped workspace: nested documents with inline databases, where table, board and calendar are three views of the same records. It has one of the largest followings in this directory, and a much smaller share of that following runs the backend itself.

Documents are the container and databases are embedded in them, with typed fields underneath; a view is a saved arrangement of one database rather than an object of its own. Kanban, grid and calendar are all first-class, workspace roles and guest links cover sharing, and the desktop and mobile builds lead the web one.

Self-hosting means running AppFlowy Cloud, the sync server, from Compose: several services over PostgreSQL, documented but not a single container. The clients are Flutter and Rust, and sync is WebSocket-based over a cloud API. There is no CalDAV or iCalendar interface, so the calendar view stays internal.

The core is AGPL and the margin is elsewhere: AI features and a vault tier are paid, and SSO and audit belong to the commercial side. Which build a capability lives in is the question to settle first, because the answer has moved with the releases. Exports are JSON, Markdown and CSV, which is adequate for documents and thinner for structured work.

records.name: Habitica
records.blurb: Habits, dailies and to-dos wrapped in a role-playing game, where parties and guilds carry the accountability a manager otherwise would.
summary: Habitica wraps habits, dailies and to-dos in a role-playing game: tasks award experience and gold, missed dailies cost health, and parties and guilds carry the accountability a manager otherwise would. It is a motivation system, and it takes the lowest mean score here because it is being measured against project tools.

There are four lists and no views: habits, dailies, to-dos and rewards. A daily repeats on a schedule the interface never draws for you, there is no board, timeline, calendar or timer, and completion rather than duration is the unit. That is the whole interface, and the narrowness is the design rather than a gap in it.

The social layer is where the work happens. Parties run quests that convert task completion into shared progress, guilds carry topic communities, and challenges let one person set tasks for many. It is a social structure rather than an organisational one, with no roles or permissions behind it.

The code is GPLv3 and self-hostable with Compose over Node.js, MongoDB and Redis, and the subscriptions are cosmetic and live on habitica.com, where nearly all of its users are. That leaves the self-hosted path thinly travelled: the bugs you hit there have fewer people ahead of you in the queue. Exports are JSON and CSV over a full REST API with user-configurable webhooks, which is more than this category usually offers.

records.name: Leantime
records.blurb: Project management aimed at non-project-managers: tasks, Kanban, timelines, retrospectives, strategy boards and native timesheets.
summary: Leantime is project management written for teams that have no project manager in them: tasks and Kanban at the front, with timelines, retrospectives, goal boards and native timesheets behind. The audience is explicit, down to onboarding that assumes you have never run a sprint.

A project carries a blueprint rather than an empty board: ideas and a strategy board, milestones on a timeline, tasks with estimates, and retrospectives at the end. Time logging sits in the core, so a timesheet comes out of the same records the board moves. The vocabulary stays plain throughout - no work items, no initiatives, no portfolio.

It is PHP over MySQL with a server-rendered interface, run from a Compose file with a web server beside it. There is no queue, cache or object store to operate, which puts it among the lighter deployments here despite the feature count. Calendars leave as iCalendar feed URLs for tasks and milestones, one way out; there is no CalDAV.

The AGPL core is the product and the commercial layer is a plugin marketplace rather than a held-back edition, which makes the boundary easier to read than most open-core arrangements. It does move, though: anything you build on a paid plugin has to be replaced before you leave. CSV, JSON and timesheet exports, a REST API and webhooks cover the exit for the core itself.

records.name: Logseq
records.blurb: An outliner over plain Markdown and Org-mode files, where the task list is a query across notes you already wrote.
summary: Logseq is an outliner over plain Markdown and Org-mode files on your own disk, where a task list is a query across notes you already wrote. It takes 5.0 for both sovereignty and portability, which is what a database made of files on your own disk is worth.

Work is captured as blocks. A block marked TODO or DOING is a task, a clock log accumulates on it while it is DOING, and queries pull them back together by page, tag, deadline or scheduled date. The daily journal is the default entry point, so tasks tend to be written where the thinking happened rather than filed somewhere separate.

Deployment is optional: a container for the self-hosted web app, a desktop build with no server at all, or the hosted browser demo reading a local folder. Opening a local graph in the browser needs the File System Access API, which Chromium implements and Firefox and Safari do not. There is no CalDAV or iCalendar interface anywhere in it.

The marketplace listed 486 plugins in August 2026, and the shape of that number matters more than its size: it extends the editor rather than reaching out to other systems. A kanban board and calendar views are in there, and neither is in core. The open question is the database rewrite, in beta for a long time with plugin compatibility against it still unsettled. The exit, meanwhile, is that there is nothing to exit: Markdown and Org-mode files, readable if Logseq never runs again.

records.name: Nextcloud Deck
records.blurb: Kanban inside Nextcloud, worth testing before deploying a second platform if Nextcloud is already in place.
summary: Deck is a Kanban board that runs as an app inside Nextcloud, beside Files, Calendar and Talk. If Nextcloud is already deployed it is the cheapest board in this directory to add; if it is not, it is the most expensive.

Cards carry due dates, labels, assignees, checklists and attachments drawn from Nextcloud Files, and boards share through the same groups that share everything else on the platform. A Gantt view was announced in June 2026, which is why older comparisons still list its absence. What is missing is the layer above the board: no portfolio, no cross-project reporting, no cost model.

The strongest reason to choose it is calendar sync. Deck cards surface through Nextcloud Tasks over CalDAV, read and write, against the same items the board shows. With Vikunja it is one of only two entries here offering a two-way standard interface, which is what makes an unmodified phone a first-class client. Time tracking is not native; a third-party app covers it.

Deployment is Nextcloud’s own, and Deck is the short step at the end of it: stand up the platform over PostgreSQL or MariaDB, then add Deck and Tasks from the app store. Identity, sharing, quotas and administration are inherited rather than implemented, which is most of why the enterprise score sits where it does. Data leaves as iCalendar and CalDAV, JSON, and CSV through companion apps, over OCS and REST APIs - but it leaves with Nextcloud rather than on its own.

records.integrationNotes: The value is in Nextcloud itself, Files and Calendar and sharing, rather than standalone connectors.

records.name: NocoDB
records.blurb: Puts grid, kanban, gallery, form and calendar views over a SQL database you already own, so the task board is a view rather than a new system of record.
records.modelSub: AGPL core + paid cloud and enterprise
summary: NocoDB puts grid, kanban, gallery, form and calendar views over a SQL database, including one you already run, so a task board becomes a view rather than a new system of record. It is the largest project here by star count and among the furthest from being a task manager out of the box.

Point it at an existing PostgreSQL or MySQL schema and it reads the tables as they stand; start from scratch and it keeps its own SQLite. Either way you get formulas, lookups, rollups, links between tables, per-view filters and sorts, and forms that write rows. Five view types over any table is a lot of interface for something that models nothing about tasks in particular.

Because the database can be yours, the data need never enter NocoDB’s storage in the first place, which is the strongest portability position in this directory. Exports are CSV, JSON and Excel, the REST API is generated from the schema with Swagger, webhooks fire per table, and Zapier, n8n and Make connectors are packaged.

The AGPL core self-hosts in full from one container, with owner, creator, editor, commenter and viewer roles per base; SSO, audit logs and row-level policy sit in the paid tiers. What it does not supply is a method. Sprints, dependencies and timelines exist only once you have modelled them, and the modelling is yours to get right.

records.name: PLANKA
records.blurb: Board-first Trello alternative. The Community edition is capable; timeline and calendar sit in the paid tiers.
summary: PLANKA is the closest self-hosted thing to Trello: lists of cards on a board, dragged between columns, with swimlanes, labels, due dates and attachments. The Community edition is a working board for a team; the timeline and calendar views sit in the paid tiers.

Board mechanics are where the effort has gone. Cards carry checklists, comments, membership and stopwatch-style time entries, notifications reach a wide set of targets, and boards move in and out as JSON. There is no portfolio layer and no dependency model, because the board is the product rather than a view onto something larger.

Deployment is two containers, the application and PostgreSQL, and nothing else: no object store, no queue, no cache. It comes up quickly and the Node.js and React stack is ordinary to operate. There is no calendar interface at all, so due dates stay inside PLANKA.

The licence is the part to read before committing. PLANKA is recorded here as source-available rather than FOSS: the editions are governed by fair-code terms rather than OSI-approved licensing, and several organisational features belong to Pro and Enterprise. The data is yours and leaves as JSON or CSV over a REST API. The software comes with conditions attached, which is precisely what the licensing column is recording.

records.name: Taiga
records.blurb: Agile-first: backlogs, sprint boards, burndowns, WIP limits and swimlanes, with no native Gantt, calendar or time tracking.
summary: Taiga is agile-first and says so by omission: backlogs, sprint boards, burndowns, WIP limits, swimlanes and epics, with no Gantt, no calendar and no time tracking anywhere in it. A team that already runs sprints needs no introduction to it; anyone who needs a timeline has finished the evaluation.

Scrum and Kanban are separate project types rather than two layouts of one. User stories carry points per role, sprints close with a burndown, and epics group stories across projects. Custom fields, custom statuses and per-project workflow configuration go deep; what is absent sits above the sprint, in portfolio, cost and governance.

Self-hosting is a multi-container Compose stack - Django and React over PostgreSQL, with RabbitMQ and Redis behind the events system - installed through an official script. It is documented, and it is not one container. The Python stack is conventional; the number of services is the cost.

It is open source throughout with nothing reserved for a paid edition, and the first-party cloud is convenience rather than leverage. A project dumps completely as JSON, with CSV beside it and a REST API and webhooks for the rest. The integration story is source control: GitHub, GitLab, Gitea and Gogs are the documented ones.

records.name: Focalboard
records.blurb: Trello-shaped boards with table, gallery and calendar views over the same cards, from the Mattermost project and now maintained by whoever turns up.
summary: Focalboard is a Trello-shaped board with Notion-shaped properties: table, gallery and calendar views over the same cards, custom fields, filters and grouping. It came out of the Mattermost project, and it is now maintained by whoever turns up.

A board is a table of cards with typed properties - select, date, person, number, text - and the four views are four ways of drawing that table. Grouping by any select property makes a different board without moving any data. Above the board there is nothing: roles are admin, editor, commenter and viewer, per board, with no organisational model over them.

The personal server is a single Docker image, or the board runs as a plugin inside an existing Mattermost, where identity and sharing come from the platform instead. MIT covers the personal server and an AGPL enterprise build sits beside it. Hosting exists only inside Mattermost Cloud, which is to say there is nowhere to buy the board on its own.

Governance is the caveat and it is a hard one. Mattermost stopped bundling the plugin in September 2023 and contributes neither features nor fixes; community commits continue into 2026 against an open call for maintainers. Plan around a roadmap that is not there, and read the exit routes as the operative feature: JSON board archives, CSV exports and a REST API are enough to leave with, which for a project in this state is what matters.

records.name: Grist
records.blurb: A relational spreadsheet with Python formulas and cell-level access rules, where the tracker is something you assemble rather than something you are given.
summary: Grist is a relational spreadsheet with Python formulas, cell-level access rules, and a document that is a SQLite file. A task tracker is one of the things you can build in it. It is not one of the things it ships.

A document holds tables, and the pages over them are assembled from widgets: a grid, a card list, a chart, a kanban widget over a status column, a calendar over a date column. Widgets link by selection, so picking a project row filters the task table beside it. Formulas are real Python evaluated in a sandbox, which puts conditional logic and rollups within reach of anyone who can write a list comprehension.

Access rules have no equal in this table. Read, update and create rights can be granted by table, by column, by row and by the value of a cell, evaluated per user, and the rule engine is in the Apache-2.0 core rather than the paid build. SSO and SCIM are Enterprise. The rest self-hosts as one container over SQLite, with no external database, queue or object store to run beside it.

The exit is unusually clean: a Grist document is a SQLite file you can download and open with anything that speaks SQLite, with CSV and Excel exports and a REST API with an interactive console beside it. Packaged Zapier, n8n and Make connectors and outgoing webhooks cover automation. The project has visible adoption in public-sector and civic-tech deployments, where that exit is the reason it was chosen.
records.bandEvidence: 11.8k GitHub stars, steady releases, and visible adoption in public-sector and civic-tech deployments.
records.integrationNotes: REST API with an interactive console, outgoing webhooks, custom widgets, and packaged Zapier, n8n and Make connectors.
records.calendarSync: None. Neither CalDAV nor an iCalendar feed.
records.dataOut: SQLite, CSV and Excel exports; REST API with an interactive console, and outgoing webhooks.
records.caveat: Not a task manager out of the box. You get a database, a formula language and the parts to build one, which is either exactly the point or immediately the problem.

deploy.review: One official container over SQLite, with no queue, cache or object store to run beside it.

use.review: Spreadsheet fluency gets you a long way; a task board is still something you have to design.

enterprise.review: Access rules down to the individual cell are the best in this table. SSO and SCIM are Enterprise.

flex.review: Widgets, Python formulas and linked views will model almost any process you can describe.

sovereignty.review: grist-core self-hosts completely; the Enterprise build adds administration rather than function.

portability.review: Your document is a SQLite file. Few exits in this field are that clean.

records.name: Kanboard
records.blurb: Deliberately minimal Kanban with SQLite by default, a plugin architecture, and almost no operational surface area.
summary: Kanboard is a minimal Kanban board with an unusually small operational footprint: one PHP application over SQLite, no build step, no JavaScript framework, MIT licensed with nothing held back. It suits teams who want the board to be dependable more than they want it to be handsome.

Behind the sparse interface is more machinery than it advertises. Swimlanes, WIP limits per column, automatic actions that fire on card events, subtasks with their own timers, a Gantt chart and a calendar are all in core. Plugins add the rest, and a plugin is PHP dropped into a directory rather than a build step.

It runs on SQLite by default, with PostgreSQL and MySQL optional, in a single container or on any PHP host. There is almost nothing to operate - no queue, no cache, no object store - and a backup is a file copy. That is why it takes 4.9 for deployment, behind only the entry with no server at all.

Calendars leave as read-only iCalendar feeds, one per project and one per user; a JSON-RPC API and webhooks cover automation. The licence is MIT, the codebase is small enough to read, and and the project has been maintained since 2014 by a contributor list in the hundreds. Very little of it would be hard to leave behind, which is the point of it.
records.bandEvidence: Long-lived, with 300+ contributors reported in project materials and a large plugin ecosystem.
records.integrationNotes: Plugins, webhooks and an API. The working count changes over time.
records.calendarSync: iCalendar subscription feeds per project and per user, one way out. No CalDAV.
records.dataOut: CSV and JSON exports; JSON-RPC API and webhooks.
records.caveat: Suits teams that want simplicity and control more than a polished interface.

use.review: Direct and unambiguous, and deliberately unpolished.

enterprise.review: The workflow core is sound. Native governance and portfolio depth are not there.

sovereignty.review: MIT, and small enough to read. Nothing constrains what you do with it.

portability.review: A permissive licence, an API and an ordinary database. Very little to leave behind.

oss.deployment: One PHP container over embedded SQLite, with PostgreSQL and MySQL optional. Almost no operational surface.
oss.stack: PHP over SQLite by default; no build step and no JavaScript framework.

records.name: Kimai
records.blurb: Timesheets first: activities, rates, budgets and invoices for teams whose tasks exist mainly to be billed.
summary: Kimai is a timesheet application with tasks attached rather than the reverse: activities under projects under customers, with rates, budgets, approvals and invoices on top. For teams whose work exists mainly to be billed, it is the shortest path from a recorded hour to a sent invoice.

Nothing in it is a card on a board. An hour is booked against an activity, inside a project, inside a customer, started on a timer or typed in afterwards, and the rest is the machinery around it: hourly and internal rates per user, customer and activity, budgets with alerts, approval workflows, and invoice templates that render to PDF from the same records.

It is a Symfony PHP application over MySQL, one Compose file, maintained since 2006, with an installation guide that has had twenty years of questions put to it. Roles run customer, user, team lead and administrator with strict visibility gates, and SSO and an audit trail are in the core rather than sold on top. A one-way iCalendar feed of the timesheet is the only calendar interface.

The commercial layer is an official plugin store, and a good part of the ecosystem lives there, including accounting and chat connectors such as Bexio, Lexoffice and Microsoft Teams. The AGPL core still tracks, budgets and invoices without reaching for the store. Exports are CSV, XLSX, PDF and JSON over a JSON REST API, with mobile and desktop clients and a CLI beside them, because getting time into an accounting system is the design goal.
records.bandEvidence: 5.0k GitHub stars, twenty years of continuity, frequent releases and an active official plugin store.
records.integrationNotes: A JSON REST API, mobile and desktop clients, a CLI, and an official store carrying accounting and chat connectors such as Bexio, Lexoffice and Microsoft Teams.
records.calendarSync: An iCalendar feed of the timesheet, one way out. No CalDAV.
records.dataOut: CSV, XLSX, PDF and JSON exports, plus invoice templates; a JSON REST API.
records.caveat: Open core by plugin. The AGPL core bills and invoices on its own, but a good deal of the ecosystem, including several accounting connectors, sits in a paid store.

records.name: Super Productivity
records.blurb: A personal task list with pomodoro timing and timeboxing that pulls its work items out of the trackers your team already runs.
summary: Super Productivity is a personal task list with a pomodoro timer and a day schedule, which pulls its work items out of the trackers a team already runs. It is single-user by design, it has no server, and it takes 5.0 for deployment because there is nothing to deploy.

The loop is the product: pick a task, start the timer, and the time log writes itself; at the end of the day the schedule shows where the hours went. Tasks arrive from a dozen named issue providers - Jira, GitHub, GitLab, OpenProject, Linear and Azure DevOps among them - and each one is called straight from your own device, with no middleware holding a copy in the middle.

There is no multi-user model at all: no roles, no shared instance, nothing to administer. That is the lowest enterprise score in the table and a description rather than a complaint. Data lives in the browser’s IndexedDB, with optional sync to WebDAV, Dropbox or a local file, so the sovereignty question resolves before it is asked.

It reads a CalDAV server as one more issue source but is not itself a CalDAV server, and the schedule timeboxes today rather than charting dependencies. Exports are JSON and CSV, plus whatever the sync target already holds as plain files. MIT, no hosted tier, 22.1k stars, and frequent releases from one maintainer with a steady contributor stream behind them.
records.bandEvidence: 22.1k GitHub stars and frequent releases, driven by one maintainer with a steady contributor stream.
records.integrationNotes: Jira, Trello, GitHub, GitLab, Gitea, Forgejo, OpenProject, Linear, ClickUp, Azure DevOps, Google Calendar and CalDAV, each called directly from your own device with no middleware in between.

records.dataOut: JSON and CSV exports, plus whatever the sync target holds; integrations with other trackers rather than an API of its own.

records.name: Taskwarrior
records.blurb: A command-line task manager with a tuneable urgency model; the browser arrives through third-party clients built on its sync protocol.
summary: Taskwarrior is a command-line task manager with a tuneable urgency model, twenty years of continuity, and no first-party web interface. It is in this directory because third-party clients built on its sync protocol reach it from a browser.

Tasks carry projects, tags, priorities, due and scheduled dates and arbitrary user-defined attributes, and urgency is a weighted sum of them with coefficients you can edit. Contexts and filters do the work a board would do elsewhere. Reports are defined in configuration and rendered in the terminal, including a calendar report that is a printout rather than a view you can schedule against.

Storage is a local database, with TaskChampion, the Rust sync implementation, as an optional server for keeping several machines in agreement. There are no roles, no organisation and no shared project, and the enterprise score of 1.2 describes a tool that was never trying to have any.

The browser route is the caveat. It comes from third parties on the documented sync protocol, including WingTask and taskwarrior_web, and the MIT licence at the head of this record covers the task engine rather than the client you would log into. Data is JSON and the native task format, with a CLI and a hook system, on a format with two decades of compatibility behind it.

records.integrationNotes: The documented TaskChampion sync protocol, a hook system, and third-party clients including WingTask and taskwarrior_web. There is no first-party web interface.

records.name: Trilium Notes
records.blurb: A scriptable hierarchical note tree. A first-party task list is in development; today a to-do is a note carrying a label.
summary: Trilium Notes is a scriptable hierarchical note tree with attributes, templates and scripting that runs inside the notes themselves. The first-party task list is still being built; until it lands, a to-do is a note wearing a label and a community script is what renders those notes as a list.

Notes nest, and the same note can appear in several places in the tree at once. Attributes - labels and relations - are the modelling primitive, templates apply structure to new notes, and scripts stored in notes run against the rest. Almost anything can be built from that, given the patience to invent the convention first.

It runs as one container with an embedded SQLite database, with desktop clients syncing to it. There is no concept of a second user: the instance is single-tenant and password-protected. That rules it out for team work and leaves it strong as a personal knowledge base with tasks inside it.

The lineage matters here, because the name outlived the repository it started in: development moved, releases resumed on a regular cadence, and 37.9k stars came across with it. Anything written about Trilium before that move describes a codebase nobody is maintaining. Data leaves as HTML, Markdown or a complete database ZIP, with a token-authenticated REST interface called ETAPI; leaving is a download.
records.bandEvidence: 37.9k GitHub stars carried over from the original project, with TriliumNext shipping regular releases since the original was archived.
records.integrationNotes: ETAPI, a token-authenticated REST interface, plus scripts that run inside notes. No packaged connectors to other task systems.
records.calendarSync: None. Neither CalDAV nor an iCalendar feed.
records.dataOut: HTML and Markdown exports, and a full database ZIP; ETAPI token-authenticated REST.
records.caveat: Barely a task manager yet. A first-party task list is in development; today a to-do list is a note with an #initTodo label and a community script behind it. The original zadam/trilium is archived - TriliumNext is the maintained continuation and the one recorded here.

flex.review: Attributes, templates and in-note scripting will build almost anything, slowly.

sovereignty.review: AGPL, self-hosted, embedded database, and the whole thing exports as one file.

portability.review: HTML, Markdown and a complete database ZIP, plus ETAPI. Leaving is a download.

records.name: Vikunja
records.blurb: Lightweight, sovereignty-first task management with list, Kanban, Gantt and table views, CalDAV, and importers from the major SaaS tools.
summary: Vikunja is task management that stays a task list: list, Kanban, table and Gantt views over tasks, labels and reminders, with CalDAV underneath and importers from the tools people are usually leaving. It is the lightest server in this directory and one of only two entries with two-way calendar sync.

The model is plain on purpose. Projects hold tasks; tasks hold subtasks, relations, labels, assignees, reminders and attachments; saved filters do the work a query language does elsewhere. There are no work items, initiatives or portfolios to learn, and little enterprise workflow configuration behind the views.

It deploys as a single Go binary on a machine you already have, or as two containers over SQLite or PostgreSQL, with nothing else required beside it. CalDAV is native and two-way against the same tasks the interface shows, which makes a phone’s built-in reminders app a client. Importers cover Todoist, Trello and Microsoft To Do.

Time tracking moved to a separate Pro tier in 2026, out of the free AGPL core, and audit and administration features sit there too. The core stays AGPL, self-hostable and exportable: a full account export as JSON with a ZIP of attachments, plus CalDAV, a REST API and webhooks. The move between Vikunja Cloud and a self-hosted instance is documented in both directions.
records.bandEvidence: Releases through 2026, established documentation, and a plugin system still growing.
records.integrationNotes: CalDAV, and importers from Todoist, Trello and Microsoft To Do. Plugins widen it further.
records.calendarSync: Native CalDAV, read and write, against the same tasks the interface shows.
records.dataOut: Full account export as JSON and a ZIP of attachments; CalDAV, REST API and webhooks.
records.caveat: Time tracking moved to Vikunja Pro in 2026, out of the free AGPL core.

records.name: Wekan
records.blurb: A ten-year-old open-source Trello with swimlanes, checklists, subtasks, colour tags and rule-based automation.
summary: Wekan is an open-source Trello that has been shipping since 2016: lists, cards, swimlanes, checklists, subtasks, colour-coded labels and rule-based automation, under MIT with no edition held back. It is one of the plainest licensing positions in this directory.

The board is deeper than the one it imitates. Swimlanes cross the lists, rules fire on card events without a plugin, and a card carries received, start, due and end dates - four date fields, and still no timer or timesheet behind them. Views cover Kanban, lists, swimlanes and a calendar.

The operational story is the caveat. Wekan is a Meteor application over MongoDB, run from Compose or a snap package, and the Meteor upgrades have been the eventful part of its history rather than the board on top of them. The application is dependable; the stack under it is where the attention goes.

Data leaves as JSON, CSV and TSV over a REST API with outgoing webhooks tested against Slack and Rocket.Chat, and a documented Trello import brings boards in. Due dates leave as a one-way iCalendar feed; there is no CalDAV. Ten years of continuous releases and 21.1k stars sit behind it, and the project was marked at the Free Software Conference Ukraine in July 2026.

records.name: Restyaboard
records.blurb: A Trello-shaped board with offline caching, card-level messaging and email-to-card, effectively frozen since 2022.
summary: Restyaboard is a Trello-shaped board with offline caching, card-level messaging and email-to-card, last tagged at 1.7.1 in March 2022. It is recorded here for completeness rather than as a recommendation.

The feature list was ahead of its moment: Kanban, list, Gantt and calendar views, offline sync, chat on cards, and mail dropped straight onto a board. Organisation admins, board managers and restricted guests cover the access model. All of it works, and all of it looks precisely like 2022.

Deployment is Docker with Nginx, PHP and PostgreSQL, and the install notes have not been revisited since the code stopped moving. The stack - PHP with a Backbone.js front end - dates the project as clearly as the interface does. A one-way iCalendar feed of card due dates is the only calendar interface.

The licence is OSL-3.0: OSI-approved, but unusual, with reciprocity terms that complicate reuse more than MIT or GPL would. The company still sells a commercial product; the open board has had no tagged release in four years, and the commits since do not add up to one. Check whether that has changed before going further, and treat CSV, JSON and the REST API as the reason it is safe to try at all.

records.name: Titra
records.blurb: Time and task tracking for studios and agencies: assignments, budgets and burn rates against client projects.
summary: Titra tracks time against tasks for studios and agencies: assignments, budgets, burn rates and client projects, with a weekly time grid as the main interface. It is a small project with a narrow remit and does not pretend to a wider one.

The unit is a booked hour. Tasks exist as things to book time against rather than cards to move, the calendar view is a time grid by day and week rather than a calendar of work, and there is no board of any kind. Project permissions and client rate masking cover the access model, which is enough for an agency and not for a department.

It is a Meteor and React application over MongoDB, deployed as one container and small enough to run and forget. A first-party hosted service exists and sells hosting rather than features: nothing is reserved out of the AGPL build.

Everything points at the handover. CSV, XLSX and JSON exports and a REST API are there to get time into an accounting system, which is the design goal rather than an afterthought. The counterweight is scale: 497 GitHub stars, the fewest in this directory, and a maintainer group small enough to count - worth weighing against how much of a billing process you would put on it.
records.bandEvidence: 497 GitHub stars and steady small-team development. A niche tool with a clear audience and little noise around it.

use.review: A time grid and a task list, with very little between you and a filled timesheet.

enterprise.review: Project permissions and client rate masking. Enough for an agency, not for a department.

flex.review: Narrow on purpose: time grid, task list, project tracking, and no views beyond them.

sovereignty.review: AGPL with nothing reserved, and the hosted service is convenience rather than leverage.

portability.review: CSV, XLSX and JSON out over a REST API, which is what an accounting handover needs.

agile.note: No board. Tasks exist as things to book time against.

calendar.note: A time grid by day and week, not a calendar of work.

oss.modelNote: AGPLv3, with hosting rather than features sold on top
oss.deployment: One container over MongoDB.
oss.capabilityNotes: Calendar view - A time grid by day and week, not a calendar of work. Agile boards, Kanban or Scrum - No board. Tasks exist as things to book time against.

records.name: Worklenz
records.blurb: Agency and services-firm workflow: client projects, billable time, task management and reporting.
summary: Worklenz is built for agencies and services firms: client projects, task boards, billable time, and the reports that turn one into an invoice. It is younger than most of this table and the commercial model around it is still settling.

Work is organised by client and project, with tasks carrying estimates, assignees and time entries, and timesheets rolling up per person and per project. Boards, lists, Gantt and a reporting section cover the views. The workflow extension depth of Redmine or OpenProject is not there, and for this audience it is not what is being bought.

It is Node.js and Angular over PostgreSQL, deployed with Docker Compose plus object storage for attachments, on a self-hosting path that is current and documented. There is no calendar interface of any kind, so deadlines and bookings stay inside the application.

The core is AGPL and the direction is commercial: a self-hosted business licence exists and its edition boundaries have moved, so the terms are worth reading in full before a deployment rather than after one. Data leaves as CSV and Excel exports of tasks, timesheets and reports, with a REST API beside them. The ecosystem is smaller than the leaders here: hundreds of forks, moving issues, continuing releases.
records.bandEvidence: Hundreds of forks, moving issues and pull requests, continuing releases, and a smaller ecosystem than the leaders.
records.integrationNotes: Modest next to Plane or OpenProject. An API and the commercial roadmap may widen it.
records.calendarSync: None. Neither CalDAV nor an iCalendar feed.
records.dataOut: CSV and Excel exports of tasks, timesheets and reports; REST API.
records.caveat: The self-hosted business-licence model and its edition boundaries are still changing.

deploy.review: A conventional web stack with a current self-hosting path, and less road behind it.

use.review: Planning and timesheets an agency team can pick up without training.

enterprise.review: Built for services firms. The enterprise licensing and admin model is still moving.

flex.review: Boards, lists, Gantt and reporting, without the workflow extension depth of Redmine or OpenProject.

sovereignty.review: The AGPL core self-hosts. Send the business-licence terms to procurement first.

portability.review: Ordinary self-hosting with the source available, on a commercial roadmap that may add dependencies.

oss.modelNote: AGPL open-core / commercial direction
oss.deployment: Docker Compose with Node.js and PostgreSQL, plus object storage for attachments.
oss.capabilityNotes: Calendar view - Not a core highlighted view.

hero.title: Commercial task managers compared
hero.lede: Pricing, features and six scored criteria for closed-source software sold as a service, with the reasoning attached.

matrix.caption: Fifty-eight commercial, closed-source task managers compared by audience, the year each launched, market presence, entry price, estimated integrations and an overall score. Expand a row for the five capability checks, the six criterion scores from 1 to 5 and the reasoning behind each one.

project.label: Product
project.tip: Name, mark and one-line description of what the product is. Sorts alphabetically, and is the one column with nothing judged in it.

model.label: Built for
model.tip: The market the vendor sells to: individuals, general teams, software teams, or large organisations buying portfolio and resource management. The vendor’s name sits beneath. Hover a tag for its definition.

community.label: Market
community.tip: An editorial band, not a measurement. Users, paying customers, revenue, headcount and ecosystem are read together, never one metric. Each band says on hover what puts a product in it.

metric.label: Paid from
metric.tip: The cheapest paid plan, per user per month, billed annually, in US dollars as published around 10 November 2026. A flat team price is shown as what each of ten people would pay, and a price in another currency is converted; both carry a ≈ with the published price beneath. A dagger marks a seat minimum or another qualification. Quote-only products sort last whichever way the column is read.

integrations.label: Integr.
integrations.tip: Estimated meaningful packaged integrations: named connectors and marketplace apps, counted as a range. An API reaches anything, so API and webhook access is described in each record rather than counted here.

year.label: Launched
year.tip: The year the product first launched publicly, as the vendor’s own history records it where it can. Age is not quality: it reads next to the market band as a measure of how long the product has had to settle.

matrix.capsTip: Five capability checks, read from the vendor’s documentation and plan pages, each three-state: native, partial, or not native. What partial means is column-specific, and every check states it in its own screen-reader text.
matrix.updated: Fifty-eight products, compiled <time datetime="2026-11-11">11 November 2026</time>. Expand a row for capabilities, scores and sources. Scores are editorial judgements on a 1-5 scale.
matrix.provenance: Market presence is an editorial band read from users, customers, revenue and headcount, not a market-share figure. Prices were read from vendor pricing pages around 10 November 2026, per user per month billed annually, in US dollars; ≈ marks a flat team price shown per person for ten people, or a converted currency; a † marks a price with a further qualification. Integration figures estimate packaged connectors and marketplace apps; APIs and webhooks are in each record.

score.tip: Unweighted mean of seven scores: the six criteria, each scored 1-5 by reading the vendor’s pricing, documentation and trust pages, and market presence, its band read as 1 (small) to 5 (very large). An editorial judgement, not a benchmark. Expand a row for all seven and the reasoning behind each one.
score.sr: Mean of the six criteria and market presence
score.critTail: Assessed against the published criteria; the expanded record includes the reasoning and research confidence.

band.name: Market presence
band.text: The market band read as a score, from Small at 1 to Very large at 5. A product more organisations pay for is likelier to stay supported, keep its integrations current and still be sold in five years.

tips.1: A small team and a small footprint. Continuity is a risk you take on yourself.
tips.2: Stable but niche: a loyal base and a small company. Expect to rely on the vendor’s support rather than on a community.
tips.3: Established, with hundreds of thousands of users and years of selling the product. Answers exist, mostly in the vendor’s own help centre.
tips.4: Millions of users, or more than a hundred thousand paying organisations. Widely known, with a large ecosystem of templates, partners and consultants.
tips.5: A category leader: tens of millions of users, or a product line of a major public company. Guides, templates and consultants are easy to find.

band.tail: Read from users, paying customers, revenue, headcount and ecosystem together, never one metric, and never the vendor’s own superlatives.

empty.search: The search reads names, vendors, audiences and the one-line descriptions. Try a shorter word, a vendor such as Atlassian or Microsoft, or clear it and browse.
empty.filters: Native time tracking, Gantt, a calendar and two-way sync for one audience rules out nearly everything, and partial support never satisfies a must-have. Loosen one filter and try again.

routes.title: Where to start
routes.note: The matrix says what each product does and costs. These are the routes the research supports.

method.title: How the scores work
method.note: Six criteria and the market band, each 1 to 5, each with a written justification. Four criteria are shared with the open-source directory; two change, because a service someone else runs raises different questions.
notes: The Score column is the unweighted mean of all seven, so the band carries one seventh of it. The directory opens by market presence, largest first. Each record also carries a Confidence value: High means pricing, features and data handling were verified on the vendor’s own current pages; Medium-high flags one remaining qualification; Medium means part of the record rests on secondary sources. Read the caveat and sources with the label.

A product sold only by quote scores low on value for money by design: a price a reader cannot see cannot be judged good value. That pulls the mean of enterprise suites down, so read their other five criteria on their own.
The two directories share a scale but not two of their criteria, so a commercial product and an open-source one are best compared on the four criteria they share, not on the mean.
method.modelsTitle: Who each product is built for
method.modelsNote: The label follows the market the vendor sells to, not every use the product can be put to. Plenty of software teams run on a general team tool, and plenty of individuals live in one built for teams.

contribute.text: If a record is wrong, send the correction with a source. Prices rise, features move between tiers, products are acquired or shut down; each correction is checked against the same criteria as everything else.
contribute.listing: Three rules: closed source, sold as a service, and usable in a web browser. A desktop-only app does not qualify, however good it is; neither does a product that has stopped selling. Nobody pays to be listed.

crosslink.title: Open-source task managers compared
crosslink.text: Twenty-five browser-based task managers whose source you can read, most of which you can run on your own server.

footer.note: A volunteer-run directory of task managers, open and commercial. Not affiliated with, endorsed by or funded by any vendor or project listed here, with one exception: Todoi is built by the directory’s maintainer.

llms.before:
## Commercial task managers

A companion page, [Commercial task managers compared](https://todoi.org/commercial-task-managers/), applies the same method to 58 closed-source task managers sold as a service and usable in a browser. One of them, Todoi, is built by this directory’s maintainer, and its record says so. Two criteria differ: value for money replaces ease of deployment, and data control replaces data sovereignty. Prices are the cheapest paid plan per user per month, billed annually, in US dollars as published around 10 November 2026. The dataset is at https://todoi.org/todoi-commercial-dataset-2026-11-10.csv.

Ordered by market presence, largest first, with alphabetical ties, matching the page.

## Notes for citation

Scores are editorial judgements published with their reasoning, not benchmark results. Cite the individual criterion and its justification rather than the mean, and cite the confidence beside the score. Every record names the date it was compiled and the sources it was compiled from.
