faqs.question: Why does a directory of open-source software list closed-source products?
faqs.answer: Most people choosing a task manager are weighing a commercial service, and the open-source options are easier to judge against the market they compete with. This page applies the same method to fifty-eight of those services. No vendor pays to be listed, and there are no affiliate links. One product, Todoi, is built by this directory’s maintainer, and its record says so.

faqs.question: Why do two criteria differ from the open-source page?
faqs.answer: Ease of deployment means little for a service someone else runs, so Value for money takes its place. Data sovereignty becomes Data control: without the source, the questions are where the data lives, which certifications back that up, whether a self-managed edition exists, and what AI features do with your content.

faqs.question: How are the prices compared?
faqs.answer: The Paid from column is the cheapest paid plan per user per month, billed annually, in US dollars as published around 10 November 2026. Monthly billing almost always costs more; each record gives both where the vendor publishes both. A flat team price is shown as what each of ten people would pay, a price in euros is converted, and both carry a ≈ with the published price beneath; a dagger marks a seat minimum or another qualification. The cheapest plan is rarely the one a growing team ends up on, and the record says which tier the limits push you towards.

faqs.question: Does a free plan mean free?
faqs.answer: It means a permanent tier with no time limit. Most cap seats, projects, storage, automations or history, and each record says where. A free trial is not a free plan, and the filter does not count one.

faqs.question: Are all fifty-eight assessed to the same depth?
faqs.answer: No. Every record carries a Confidence value. Each product was researched from the vendor’s own pricing, documentation and trust pages, checked against the live pages by a second reader, then edited against the rest of the set so that a 4 means the same thing in every row. Where a fact rests on a secondary source, the record says so.

faqs.question: How current is this?
faqs.answer: Compiled on 11 November 2026. Commercial prices and plans change several times a year, far more often than open-source licences do, so check the vendor’s own page before you buy. Each record’s caveat names what was changing when it was written.

routes.case: A 50-5,000 person organisation that needs SSO, audit logs and a say over where the data lives
routes.pick: Start with Asana, monday work management and Smartsheet. All three sell SAML, provisioning and audit logging on their enterprise tiers, Smartsheet partly as add-ons. Residency is where they differ: Asana sells it on Enterprise+, monday fixes the region from the first user’s location, and Smartsheet keeps separate EU and Australian regions.

routes.case: An organisation already paying for Microsoft 365
routes.pick: Try Microsoft Planner before buying anything else. Basic Planner comes with the suites; Planner Plan 1 at $10 adds Gantt timelines, sprints and goals. Microsoft To Do keeps each person’s own list beside it.

routes.case: A software team running sprints, backlogs and releases
routes.pick: Jira for configurable workflows and the largest marketplace; Linear for speed and an EU region on every plan. YouTrack is the cheapest here at $4.50, free up to ten users, and still sold as a server you run yourself. Azure Boards if the code already lives in Azure DevOps.

routes.case: Data that must stay in the EU, or on your own servers
routes.pick: YouTrack, Azure Boards, Celoxis and Teamhood all offer an edition you can run on-premise; Bitrix24 does too, but read its record on jurisdiction first. For EU cloud hosting by default, MeisterTask runs in Frankfurt. If control is the deciding requirement, start with the open-source directory instead.

routes.case: A small team on a tight budget
routes.pick: Zoho Projects at $4 a seat brings Gantt, timesheets and issue tracking. Freedcamp at $1.49 and Plaky at $3.99 are cheaper still. Trello’s free plan works until the eleventh collaborator.

routes.case: A team that thinks in boards
routes.pick: Trello is still the reference board. MeisterTask adds native time tracking and German hosting; Favro lets the same cards sit on boards, sheets and roadmaps across teams. Businessmap for Kanban with WIP limits at department scale, from fifteen seats.

routes.case: One person, a to-do list and several devices
routes.pick: Todoist for fast capture and dependable sync. TickTick if a calendar, habits and a focus timer belong in the same app. Microsoft To Do or Google Tasks if free matters more than features and the account already exists.

routes.case: Planning each day against a calendar
routes.pick: Sunsama for a deliberate daily plan; Akiflow to pull tasks from many tools into one inbox first; Motion to let software place the tasks in the calendar for you. Tweek if a paper-like week is all you want.

routes.case: Documents, databases and tasks in the same place
routes.pick: Notion is the default and the broadest. Coda (Superhuman Docs) if the documents should compute. Airtable for relational data that outgrew a spreadsheet, now owned by Bending Spoons. Fibery for product teams who want to model their own objects.

routes.case: An agency or studio billing client hours
routes.pick: Productive ties tasks to budgets, resourcing and invoices; Teamwork.com is project management built around client work. Paymo for freelancers and small studios, from $5.90 for one person.

routes.case: A project manager who lives in Gantt charts
routes.pick: GanttPRO for critical path and baselines from $8; TeamGantt for a flat account price and a gentler learning curve. Celoxis when the Gantt has to roll up into a portfolio with resource capacity.

routes.case: Client work on a flat bill, without counting seats
routes.pick: Basecamp for to-dos, message boards and chat per project, with clients inside. ProofHub at $45 a month for unlimited users, if Gantt and proofing matter more than polish.

revisions.text: First publication: fifty-seven products, each researched from the vendor’s own pricing, documentation and trust pages, then checked against the live pages by a second reader. Upbase was researched and dropped: its pricing page is live, but its own feedback board holds months of unanswered reports of failed sign-ins and missing support replies, so continued sale could not be confirmed.
Todoi added, which makes fifty-eight products. It is built by this directory’s maintainer and scored against the same criteria as the rest; its record states the connection.

records.name: Adobe Workfront
records.blurb: Enterprise work management for marketing and creative operations: projects, requests, proofing, timesheets and portfolio planning, sold by quote.
summary: Adobe Workfront runs projects, incoming requests, proofing and approvals, timesheets and portfolio planning in one tenant. It is bought by large marketing, creative and operations departments, often alongside Adobe’s Creative Cloud and Experience Cloud.

Work is organised as portfolios, programs, projects, tasks and issues, with Gantt charts that show predecessors and the critical path, Kanban and Scrum boards, calendar reports and a resource planner. Workfront Planning adds a separate record-based layer for campaign and strategy planning. Calendar sync is now missing: the legacy Home calendar’s Outlook link was removed in October 2024 and the Outlook add-in stopped working in October 2025.

There is no published price and no free plan. Adobe sells Workflow Select, Prime and Ultimate packages by quote, with Standard, Light and Contributor licences; strategic portfolio planning and environment promotion start at Prime, Data Connect and business rules at Ultimate, and Planning and Fusion are separate purchases.

Workfront falls under Adobe Experience Cloud’s SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001 scope, with data held in the US or in the EU (Ireland, the Netherlands, Germany) as set in the contract. AI Assistant requires a signed Adobe Gen AI agreement and is turning into CX Enterprise Coworker from September 2026. Leaving means row-capped report exports or the REST API.
records.bandEvidence: More than 3,000 customers and one million users when Adobe agreed to buy it in November 2020 (KMWorld, 12 November 2020); now a product line of Adobe, a large public company.
records.integrationNotes: Workfront Fusion, Adobe’s own integration platform, lists over 70 connectors (Adobe Experience Manager, Creative Cloud, Salesforce, Jira, Slack, Microsoft Teams among them) and is metered by operations; a full REST API and event subscriptions sit beside it, and an MCP server was added in 2026.
records.calendarSync: None current. The Outlook two-way sync on the legacy Home calendar went with Legacy Home in October 2024, and Workfront for Outlook stopped working when Microsoft disabled legacy Exchange tokens on 1 October 2025. No Google Calendar integration or iCal feed is documented.
records.dataOut: Reports and lists export to PDF, Excel (.xls up to 65,000 rows, .xlsx up to 100,000), CSV and tab-delimited (50,000 rows); dashboards only to PDF. Full REST API; Data Connect warehouse access on Ultimate. Kick-Starts import and export via Excel.
records.caveat: Prices are never published, and Adobe reorganised packaging into separate Workflow, Planning and Automation purchases, so quotes from older comparisons may not match what is sold in 2026.

value.review: Every package and licence type is quote-only, with no free plan and automation through Fusion metered separately.

use.review: Access levels, licence types, custom forms and templates need a trained administrator before a team is productive.

enterprise.review: Adobe Admin Console identity, granular access levels, portfolios, programs, resource planning and Experience Cloud certifications.

flex.review: Gantt with critical path, boards, calendar reports, dashboards, custom forms, Fusion automation and a separate Planning product.

control.review: SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001 under Experience Cloud, US or EU hosting set at contract, but no self-managed edition.

portability.review: Report exports to Excel, CSV and TSV stop at 50,000 to 100,000 rows; the REST API is the realistic route out.

commercial.vendor: Adobe Inc. Public company (NASDAQ: ADBE), headquartered in San Jose, California, US; Adobe bought Workfront of Lehi, Utah for $1.5 billion in December 2020.
commercial.yearNote: 2001. Release of @task, the product AtTask sold before renaming itself Workfront in 2015.
commercial.priceNote: Adobe publishes no prices: Workflow Select, Prime and Ultimate packages are sold by quote, with Standard, Light and Contributor licences priced separately.
commercial.freePlanNote: No free plan; Adobe offers demos, and a free 60-day Workfront Planning trial ran from 2 March to 1 May 2026 for existing Workflow customers.
commercial.plans: Workflow Select, Workflow Prime and Workflow Ultimate, plus Planning Select, Prime and Ultimate and Workfront Fusion automation, all quote-only; older customers may still hold the legacy Select, Prime and Ultimate packages.
commercial.hosting: Adobe-run multi-tenant clusters in cloud providers’ data centres. Adobe’s Experience Cloud hosting-locations page (updated 5 November 2026) shows Workfront core processing and storage sites in Oregon, California, Iowa and Virginia in the US and in Ireland, the Netherlands and Germany in the EU, with the location provisioned at contract signing. No Asia-Pacific site, and no self-managed or on-premise edition.
commercial.security: Covered by Adobe Experience Cloud’s SOC 2 Type II, SOC 3, ISO 27001:2022, ISO 27017 and ISO 27018 certifications and HIPAA-ready status; not FedRAMP. SSO and user provisioning through the Adobe Admin Console on every package; environment promotion needs Prime or Ultimate, and business rules and Data Connect need Workflow Ultimate. Customer-managed encryption keys are not documented.
commercial.platforms: Web; Adobe Workfront apps for iOS and Android; Workfront View for iPad.
commercial.ai: AI Assistant on Select or higher with a Standard licence and a signed Adobe Gen AI agreement; it summarises work and writes formulas, and is being replaced by CX Enterprise Coworker from September 2026. AI Collaborators (agents assignable to tasks) became generally available in August 2026. Adobe says customer data is not used to train the Azure OpenAI models behind AI Assistant.

records.name: Asana
records.blurb: Work management for teams: tasks and projects shown as lists, boards, calendars and timelines, with portfolios, goals and AI agents on top.
summary: Asana organises work as tasks inside projects, with the same task able to sit in several projects at once. It is sold to whole organisations that want one shared place for team plans, from marketing calendars to cross-functional launches.

Every project can be shown as a list, board, calendar, timeline or Gantt chart, and portfolios and goals roll projects up for managers. Rules, forms and custom fields handle routine workflow. Since 2025 Asana has added AI Teammates and AI Studio, which run agents and automations against a monthly allowance of requests and credits.

The free Personal plan was cut to two users in November 2025, so a team of three must pay from day one. Starter at $10.99 a seat adds timeline and automations; time tracking, approvals and advanced reporting sit on Advanced at $24.99. Above five users seats are bought in steps of 5, then 10 above 30 users, and AI use beyond the included 5 requests per user per month (up to 50 per account below Enterprise) is charged at $0.50 to $0.60 per request.

Asana holds SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001, 27017, 27018 and 27701 certificates. Data residency in Europe, Australia or Japan, customer-managed encryption keys and audit logs come with Enterprise+, and Asana states that neither it nor its AI partners train models on customer data. Projects export to CSV or JSON, but the full organisation export is Enterprise+ only, so leaving a smaller plan means working through the API.
records.bandEvidence: Asana reported revenue of $790.8 million for fiscal 2026 (year to 31 January 2026), with 25,928 customers spending $5,000 or more a year, per its results release of 2 March 2026.
records.integrationNotes: The app directory lists several hundred apps, including Slack, Microsoft Teams, Google Drive, Salesforce, Jira Cloud, GitHub, Zoom, Power BI, Zapier and Claude; a public REST API with webhooks is documented at developers.asana.com.
records.calendarSync: One-way: iCal subscription links for a project or My Tasks (tasks need a due date), and an Outlook Calendar integration that sends Asana changes to Outlook but not back. Available on all plans.
records.dataOut: Per-project CSV (no comments or attachments) and JSON export; a full organisation export as JSON, with optional attachments, only on Enterprise+ and legacy Enterprise. Public REST API with webhooks; CSV importer.
records.caveat: Asana cut the free plan to two users in November 2025 and is moving older 10-user free workspaces to the same limit, so free-tier reviews from before then are out of date.

value.review: Free for only two people since late 2025, then $10.99 a seat with timeline, and $24.99 for time tracking.

use.review: Tasks, sections and My Tasks are quick to learn; portfolios, goals and rules take deliberate setup.

enterprise.review: SAML and SCIM on Enterprise, audit logs, SIEM and residency on Enterprise+, admin console and ISO 27001 certification.

flex.review: List, board, calendar, timeline, Gantt, dashboards, portfolios, forms, rules and custom fields, mostly from Starter up.

control.review: Data residency in Europe, Australia or Japan and customer-held keys through EKM, both on Enterprise+ only.

portability.review: Project CSV omits comments; a full organisation JSON export with attachments is reserved for Enterprise+ admins.

sync.note: One-way only: an iCal subscription of a project or My Tasks, and an Outlook Calendar integration that pushes Asana changes to events but not back.

commercial.vendor: Asana, Inc. Publicly listed on the NYSE (ASAN); headquartered in San Francisco, United States.
commercial.yearNote: 2011. Public launch of the web app in November 2011; the company was founded in 2008.
commercial.priceNote: Starter, per user per month billed annually; $13.49 billed monthly. Paid plans start at 2 seats, added one at a time up to 5 users, then in steps of 5 up to 30, 10 up to 100, 25 up to 500 and 50 beyond.
commercial.priceDagger: Starter, per user per month billed annually; $13.49 billed monthly. Paid plans start at 2 seats, added one at a time up to 5 users, then in steps of 5 up to 30, 10 up to 100, 25 up to 500 and 50 beyond.
commercial.freePlanNote: Personal is free for 1 or 2 people with unlimited tasks and projects in list, board and calendar views; no timeline, automations, custom fields or dashboards.
commercial.plans: Personal free (up to 2 users); Starter $10.99 annual or $13.49 monthly; Advanced $24.99 annual or $30.49 monthly; Enterprise and Enterprise+ by quote.
commercial.hosting: Asana-operated cloud, US by default; data residency in Europe, Australia or Japan on Enterprise+. No self-managed or on-premise edition.
commercial.security: SOC 2 Type II, SOC 3, ISO/IEC 27001, 27017, 27018 and 27701, CSA STAR Level 1, HIPAA support. SAML SSO and SCIM on Enterprise; audit logs, SIEM integration and EKM on Enterprise+.
commercial.platforms: Web, iOS, Android, desktop apps for macOS and Windows.
commercial.ai: Asana AI, AI Teammates and AI Studio on all paid plans with 5 requests per user per month (capped per account) and monthly AI Studio credits; extra requests are paid. Asana states it does not use customer data for training and contractually bars its AI partners from doing so.

records.name: Azure Boards
records.blurb: Work tracking inside Azure DevOps: backlogs, Kanban boards, sprints, queries and delivery plans, tied to repos and pipelines.
summary: Azure Boards is the work-tracking part of Microsoft’s Azure DevOps, the successor to Team Foundation Server. It suits software teams already on Azure, GitHub or Visual Studio who want backlogs and sprints beside their code and pipelines.

Work items follow Agile, Scrum, CMMI or custom processes and appear in backlogs, Kanban boards, sprint taskboards and saved queries; Delivery Plans show up to 20 team backlogs on a timeline with dependencies, and dashboards and Power BI handle reporting. There is no calendar view, and time is tracked as remaining and completed hours rather than with timesheets.

Basic access is free for 5 users and then $6 a seat a month, billed through Azure. Unlimited Stakeholders are free and can edit work items and move cards on a board, but cannot reorder backlogs, plan sprints or configure boards, so whoever plans the work needs a paid seat. Visual Studio and GitHub Enterprise licences include Basic.

Organisations choose one of eight geographies, from the EU to India, and Azure DevOps Server still ships for on-premise use, with Patch 9 released in October 2026. Microsoft lists ISO 27001, SOC 2 Type II, HIPAA and C5. AI arrives through GitHub Copilot, which can turn a work item into a draft pull request. Leaving is done by query exports or the API.
records.bandEvidence: A service line of Microsoft, a public company; the Visual Studio Marketplace lists 5,436 Azure DevOps extensions, 1,698 of them for Azure Boards (November 2026); Microsoft publishes no separate Azure DevOps user count.
records.integrationNotes: The Visual Studio Marketplace lists 1,698 extensions in the Azure Boards category, plus first-party links to GitHub, Microsoft Teams, Slack, Power BI and Excel; full REST APIs, service hooks and an Azure DevOps MCP Server.
records.calendarSync: None. Work items do not publish to Google or Outlook calendars, and there is no iCal feed; Microsoft’s Team Calendar extension tracks sprints and days off rather than work items.
records.dataOut: Query results export to CSV and import back for bulk edits; Excel integration publishes flat lists and hierarchies; Analytics views feed Power BI. Full REST APIs and service hooks. The Data Migration Tool moves Server collections into Services; whole-organisation moves elsewhere need Marketplace tools or the API.
records.caveat: The audit log is still in public preview and only works for Entra ID-backed organisations, and free Stakeholder seats can edit work items and move cards but cannot reorder backlogs or plan sprints.

value.review: Five free Basic users, unlimited free Stakeholders and $6 a seat after that, with repos and pipelines in the same licence.

use.review: Process templates, area and iteration paths and query-driven views need a configured project before a team is comfortable.

enterprise.review: Entra ID sign-in and conditional access, granular permissions, audit streaming, multi-organisation billing and ISO, SOC, C5 and IRAP coverage.

flex.review: Backlogs, boards, taskboards, delivery plans, queries, dashboards, Power BI views and custom processes; no calendar or list-style planner.

control.review: Eight data geographies chosen per organisation, and Azure DevOps Server remains on sale for fully self-managed hosting.

portability.review: Query results export to CSV and Excel and the REST API is complete, but no one-click export of a whole organisation exists.

tt.note: Tasks carry Original Estimate, Remaining Work and Completed Work fields feeding capacity and burndown, but there is no timer or timesheet; those need Marketplace extensions.

commercial.vendor: Microsoft. Publicly listed (NASDAQ: MSFT); headquartered in Redmond, Washington, USA. Azure Boards is part of the Azure DevOps Services suite.
commercial.yearNote: 2018. Launched as Azure Boards on 10 September 2018 within Azure DevOps, succeeding Visual Studio Team Services and the work tracking of Team Foundation Server.
commercial.priceNote: Azure DevOps Basic, per user per month after the first 5 free users, billed monthly through an Azure subscription; no annual rate is published.
commercial.freePlanNote: The first 5 Basic users are free with Boards, Repos, one Pipelines job and 2 GiB of Artifacts; unlimited free Stakeholders can view boards and backlogs, add and edit work items and move cards, but cannot reorder backlogs, bulk edit, plan sprints or configure boards.
commercial.plans: Stakeholder free; Basic free for 5 users, then $6 per user per month; Basic + Test Plans $52 per user per month. Visual Studio subscribers and GitHub Enterprise users get Basic at no extra charge.
commercial.hosting: Azure datacentres in a geography chosen per organisation: Australia, Brazil, Canada, Asia Pacific, EU, India, UK or US, movable later; profile data follows user location and tokens stay in the US. Azure DevOps Server is the self-managed on-premise edition, patched through October 2026.
commercial.security: ISO 27001:2022, ISO 27018:2019, SOC 1 Type II, SOC 2 Type II, HIPAA with BAA, EU Model Clauses, Germany C5, Australia IRAP and ENS Spain. Sign-in through Microsoft Entra ID with its SSO and conditional access; audit log (in public preview) requires Entra-backed organisations and keeps events 90 days, with streaming to Splunk or Azure.
commercial.platforms: Web, with Visual Studio and Excel clients; no official mobile app for Boards was found. Azure DevOps Server runs on Windows Server for self-hosting.
commercial.ai: GitHub Copilot integration starts Copilot’s coding agent from a work item to create a branch and draft pull request; it requires a GitHub Copilot subscription and GitHub repositories. The Azure DevOps MCP Server, hosted in Europe and the US, passes data through without storing it.

records.name: Google Tasks
records.blurb: Free, minimal to-do list built into Gmail, Google Calendar and the Workspace side panel, with lists, subtasks, due dates and repeats.
summary: Google Tasks is a bare to-do list that lives inside Gmail, Google Calendar and the Workspace side panel, with mobile apps for Android and iOS. It suits people who already plan their day in Google Calendar and want tasks beside their events, not a separate system.

A task has a title, details, a start date and time with a duration, a deadline, a repeat rule, a star and subtasks, and sits in a list. Dated tasks show on the Calendar grid, an email can become a task, and Workspace users can assign group tasks in Chat spaces and Docs. There are no labels, priorities, shared lists, board or timeline.

There is nothing to buy: a personal Google account gets the whole product. Organisations get it with any Workspace edition, from Business Starter at $7 a user per month on an annual plan, which adds administrator control rather than task features.

For Workspace customers Tasks data is covered by Google’s ISO 27001 and SOC 2 scope and by data region policies on Business Standard and above; Gemini can create tasks from any Workspace side panel since September 2026, and Google says prompts are not used for training without permission. Leaving is simple but thin: Takeout gives JSON for the whole account, there is no CSV, and nothing imports in.
records.bandEvidence: Google publishes no Tasks user count; the service ships inside Gmail, Google Calendar, Chat, Drive and Docs for every Google account and Workspace customer, a product line of Alphabet (checked November 2026).
records.integrationNotes: Gmail (email to task), Google Calendar, Chat spaces, Docs, Drive, Keep reminders and Gemini; third parties connect through the public Google Tasks REST API, which has no webhooks.
records.calendarSync: Native: tasks with dates appear in Google Calendar on web and mobile, and edits in either place apply to the same task. Repeating tasks show a limited number of upcoming instances. No Outlook sync and no iCal feed.
records.dataOut: Google Takeout exports the whole account’s Tasks as JSON (third-party guides disagree on whether it is one file or one per list), with titles, notes, due dates, completion, order and subtask links; no CSV and no scheduled backups. The Google Tasks REST API reads and writes lists and tasks. No importers.
records.caveat: Google Tasks has had no official feature announcements in 2026 beyond a widget redesign; a search bar and a “Plan your day” view have only appeared in app teardowns.

value.review: Free with any Google account and already included in every Workspace plan, with no caps a person is likely to meet.

use.review: The simplest tool here: a list, a date and a star, reachable from the Gmail and Calendar side panel.

enterprise.review: Workspace admins can switch Tasks on or off and apply SSO and data regions, but Tasks itself has no roles or reporting.

flex.review: Lists, subtasks, stars, deadlines and a calendar display; no labels, priorities, board, custom fields or automation.

control.review: Workspace lists Tasks under ISO 27001 and SOC 2 and data regions from Business Standard; personal accounts get no region choice.

portability.review: Google Takeout gives a JSON export of every list and the REST API is free, but there is no CSV or importer.

commercial.vendor: Google LLC, a subsidiary of Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ: GOOGL). Publicly traded, headquartered in Mountain View, California, USA.
commercial.yearNote: 2008. Launched as a Gmail Labs feature in December 2008; the standalone mobile app followed in April 2018.
commercial.priceNote: No paid tier of its own. Free with any Google account; organisations get admin control, data regions and Gemini features through Google Workspace, from Business Starter at $7 per user per month on an annual plan ($8.40 flexible).
commercial.freePlanNote: Every Tasks feature is free with a Google account, up to 100,000 tasks in total and 20,000 open tasks per list; group tasks in Chat spaces and assigning from Docs need an eligible Workspace account.
commercial.plans: Free with a personal Google account; included in every Google Workspace edition (Business Starter $7, Standard $14, Plus $22 per user per month on annual plans), where the administrator controls access.
commercial.hosting: Google’s own data centres. Workspace Business Standard and Plus, Enterprise, Frontline and Education Standard/Plus editions can apply a data region policy to Tasks data at rest; personal accounts have no choice. No self-managed edition.
commercial.security: Google lists Workspace services including Tasks in scope for ISO 27001, 27017, 27018 and SOC 1, 2 and 3. SSO, MFA and audit sit at the Google Workspace account level; administrators control access to Tasks, but Tasks has no roles of its own.
commercial.platforms: Web (inside Google Calendar and the side panel of Gmail, Chat, Drive, Docs, Sheets and Slides), Android, iOS and ChromeOS. No desktop app for Windows, macOS or Linux.
commercial.ai: Gemini in the Workspace side panels can create reminders and to-do lists in Google Tasks since September 2026, on Business and Enterprise Standard and Plus and on Google AI Pro and Ultra. Google states Workspace prompts are customer data and not used for training without permission.

records.name: Jira
records.blurb: Issue and project tracker built around configurable workflows, with backlog, board, timeline, list and calendar views and a 6,000-app marketplace.
summary: Jira tracks work as issues, now called work items, moving through workflows that an administrator defines, and it remains the default tracker in large software organisations. Atlassian also sells it to marketing, operations and other business teams on the same plans.

Every plan has backlog, board, list, timeline, calendar and summary views, custom fields and workflows, and JQL queries that feed dashboards and reports. The timeline shows dependencies within one project; plans across projects, capacity and scenario modelling are Premium. What it lacks out of the box is calendar sync and a timesheet, both of which arrive through the Marketplace.

The free plan stops at 10 users and 2 GB. Prices rose by about 7% on 13 October 2026: Standard is $9.70 per user a month billed monthly for the first 100 users, about $7.92 billed annually, and Premium $19.60. Rovo AI is included on paid plans with monthly credit allowances (25, 70 and 150 per user); SSO and SCIM need an Atlassian Guard subscription below Enterprise.

Data can be pinned to 11 residency locations from Standard upwards. Since 17 August 2026 Atlassian uses de-identified, aggregated metadata from Free, Standard and Premium sites to improve its apps and AI features, and only Enterprise can switch that off; in-app content is also contributed by default on Free and Standard unless an admin turns it off. Leaving is realistic: CSV, XML and Word exports, a full backup with attachments and complete APIs.
records.bandEvidence: Atlassian reported FY2026 revenue of $6,572 million and 350,000+ customers (Q4 FY2026 results, 6 August 2026), with Jira as its flagship product line.
records.integrationNotes: The Atlassian Marketplace lists more than 6,000 Cloud apps (October 2026), including Tempo, GitHub, GitLab, Slack, Microsoft Teams and Figma; public REST APIs, webhooks, the Forge app platform and a Rovo MCP server on paid plans.
records.calendarSync: None native. The calendar view shows work items by date inside Jira only; Google, Outlook or iCal sync needs a third-party Marketplace app.
records.dataOut: Search results export to CSV or Excel CSV (all or current fields, up to 10,000 items), XML, and Word (descriptions and comments included, about 150 items at a time). Backup Manager produces a full XML site backup including comments, sprints and configuration, with attachments optional (48 hours between such backups); automation rules and app data are excluded. REST APIs and webhooks on all plans; direct importers for Asana and Trello, plus CSV and JSON import.
records.caveat: Jira Data Center stopped selling to new customers on 30 March 2026 and goes read-only on 28 March 2029, so Cloud is now the only edition a new buyer can choose.

value.review: Ten free users and Standard at about $7.92 a user billed annually, but advanced planning needs Premium and SSO needs Atlassian Guard.

use.review: Schemes, workflows, screens and JQL reward an administrator; newcomers face unfamiliar terms before the first sprint.

enterprise.review: SAML SSO and SCIM through Guard, audit logs, sandboxes, 150 sites, Atlassian Analytics and FedRAMP Moderate Government Cloud.

flex.review: Custom workflows and fields on every plan, six views, JQL dashboards, rule automation and 6,000 Marketplace apps.

control.review: Residency across 11 locations from Standard, but Data Center stopped selling to new customers in March 2026.

portability.review: CSV export to 10,000 items, a full XML site backup with attachments and complete REST APIs; the backup only restores into Jira.

commercial.vendor: Atlassian. Publicly listed (NASDAQ: TEAM); founded in Sydney, Australia, in 2002, incorporated in Delaware since 2022, with headquarters in Sydney and San Francisco.
commercial.yearNote: 2002. First release of Jira as downloadable software in 2002, the year Atlassian was founded; Jira Cloud followed later.
commercial.priceNote: Standard billed annually at $950 a year for the 10-user tier (about $7.92 per user per month; $9,700 for 100 users); monthly billing is $9.70 per user for users 1-100. Prices from 13 October 2026.
commercial.priceDagger: Standard billed annually at $950 a year for the 10-user tier (about $7.92 per user per month; $9,700 for 100 users); monthly billing is $9.70 per user for users 1-100. Prices from 13 October 2026.
commercial.freePlanNote: Up to 10 users with 2 GB storage, every core view, 150 automation steps a month and community support; no Rovo AI, permissions or audit log.
commercial.plans: Free for up to 10 users; Standard $9.70 per user a month billed monthly, or $950 a year for 10 users (about $7.92 per user a month); Premium $19.60 per user billed monthly, or $1,950 a year for 10 users; Enterprise annual only, with published list prices from $179,000 a year for 1,000 users. Monthly per-user rates fall in higher user bands.
commercial.hosting: Atlassian Cloud on AWS. Data residency on Standard, Premium and Enterprise in Australia, Canada, EU, Germany, India, Japan, Singapore, South Korea, Switzerland, UK and USA. Jira Data Center (self-managed) ended sales to new customers on 30 March 2026 and reaches end of life on 28 March 2029; Jira Server lost support on 15 February 2024.
commercial.security: SOC 2 Type II reports, ISO/IEC 27001 and 27018 (scope varies by product), PCI DSS and a GDPR DPA; Atlassian Government Cloud holds FedRAMP Moderate (March 2025). SSO, SCIM and AD sync via Atlassian Guard Standard, included only on Enterprise; site audit logs from Standard, user-activity audit logs on Enterprise. BYOK is closed to new enrolment and replaced by customer-managed keys.
commercial.platforms: Web, iOS and Android. The official Jira Cloud for Mac app is no longer supported.
commercial.ai: Rovo Search, Chat and Agents on Standard, Premium and Enterprise, metered by monthly credits (25, 70 and 150 per user); not on Free. Atlassian says its LLM providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and self-hosted open models) do not store or train on inputs. Separately, from 17 August 2026 Atlassian uses contributed data, de-identified and aggregated, to improve its apps and AI experiences: metadata is always contributed on Free, Standard and Premium and can be turned off only on Enterprise; in-app data is on by default on Free and Standard (admins can turn it off) and off by default on Premium and Enterprise.

records.name: Microsoft Planner
records.blurb: Microsoft 365’s task and project planner: boards and schedules in every suite, with Gantt timelines, sprints and goals from Planner Plan 1.
summary: Microsoft Planner is the task and project tool inside Microsoft 365, reached from the web, Teams and Outlook. Since August 2025 it also carries what used to be Project for the web, so one app now spans a team’s shared board and a scheduled project.

Basic plans give tasks with buckets, checklists, labels and attachments in grid, board, schedule and charts views, plus My Day and My Tasks. Premium plans add a timeline (Gantt) view with dependencies, sprints and backlogs, goals, custom fields and a people view; Plan 3 adds critical path, baselines, roadmaps and an assignments view. There is no time tracking, and premium plans top out at 3,000 tasks each.

Most organisations already have basic Planner through a Microsoft 365 or Office 365 suite. Planner Plan 1 costs $10 per user per month paid annually and Planner and Project Plan 3 costs $30; Planner’s subscriptions page now lists only those two premium plans, and Project Online retired on 30 September 2026. Copilot and the Planner Agent need a separate Microsoft 365 Copilot licence.

Basic plan data sits in Azure in the tenant’s geography and premium plans in Dataverse, under Microsoft’s certifications and data protection addendum; Planner does not take part in Advanced Data Residency or support customer-managed keys. Leaving means Excel exports, an admin PowerShell JSON export or the Graph API.
records.bandEvidence: Bundled with Microsoft 365 Business Basic, Standard and Premium, Office 365 E1, E3 and E5 and Microsoft 365 A1 (Microsoft Learn, October 2026); Microsoft publishes no Planner-only user count.
records.integrationNotes: Built into Teams, Outlook, To Do, SharePoint and Loop, with Power Automate flows and Power BI reporting on premium plans; the Planner API in Microsoft Graph covers basic plans, premium plans live in Dataverse, and a Planner MCP server is documented.
records.calendarSync: One-way iCalendar publishing of a plan’s schedule to the Outlook calendar (any iCal client can subscribe); assigned tasks also show in Microsoft To Do. No Google Calendar sync and nothing flows back.
records.dataOut: Export a plan to Excel from the web app; global admins can export a user’s plans as JSON with the Export-PlannerUserContent PowerShell cmdlet. Planner API in Microsoft Graph for basic plans; premium plan data is reachable through Dataverse. Direct .mpp import was removed when Project for the web retired.
records.caveat: Microsoft’s own price pages blocked automated access for this review; the $10 and $30 figures are Microsoft’s list prices as quoted in October 2026, and no formal end-of-sale notice for Plan 5 was found.

value.review: Boards come free with most Microsoft 365 suites, but timelines cost $10 a seat and critical path $30.

use.review: Basic plans are a card board inside Teams and Outlook that most Microsoft 365 users can pick up unaided.

enterprise.review: Entra ID sign-in, Purview audit logs and eDiscovery, but no Planner admin roles and eDiscovery only for basic group plans.

flex.review: Grid, board, schedule, charts, timeline, people and goals views, sprints and custom fields, with Power Automate behind premium plans.

control.review: Data follows the tenant’s geography (Europe, Americas, Asia-Pacific, Australia, Canada, Japan or India), with no residency commitment or customer-managed keys.

portability.review: Export to Excel per plan, admin JSON export per user and the Graph API; .mpp import was removed in 2025.

sync.note: A plan’s schedule can be published as an iCalendar feed into Outlook; it is one-way and there is no Google Calendar sync.

commercial.vendor: Microsoft Corporation. Public company (NASDAQ: MSFT), headquartered in Redmond, Washington, US.
commercial.yearNote: 2016. General availability in Office 365 on 6 June 2016; Project for the web was folded into it on 1 August 2025.
commercial.priceNote: Planner Plan 1, per user per month paid annually as listed by Microsoft in October 2026; basic Planner comes with most Microsoft 365 business and enterprise suites at no extra charge.
commercial.freePlanNote: No standalone free plan; basic Planner (grid, board, schedule and charts views) is included in Microsoft 365 Business Basic and higher suites, but timeline, goals and sprints need Plan 1.
commercial.plans: Basic Planner inside Microsoft 365 and Office 365 suites; Planner Plan 1 at $10 and Planner and Project Plan 3 at $30 per user per month paid annually. Planner and Project Plan 5 (formerly $55) is still named in Microsoft’s Project for the web service description but no longer on Planner’s subscriptions page, which lists only Plan 1 and Plan 3.
commercial.hosting: Microsoft Azure. Basic plans are stored by the tenant’s default geography: Europe, Americas or Asia-Pacific macro-regions, with local storage for Australia, Canada, India and Japan (UK tenants map to Europe); Microsoft makes no specific residency commitment for Planner and it does not take part in Advanced Data Residency. Premium plans are stored in Dataverse. No on-premise edition (Project Server is a separate product).
commercial.security: Covered by Microsoft 365’s audit reports on the Service Trust Portal, the Product Terms and the Data Protection Addendum. Sign-in through Microsoft Entra ID with its SSO and provisioning; Purview audit logs on all plans, eDiscovery only for basic group plans, no retention policies, and Purview needs an E5-class licence.
commercial.platforms: Web, Planner in Teams (Windows, macOS, Linux via the Teams client), Outlook integration, iOS and Android apps.
commercial.ai: Copilot in Planner and the Planner Agent (Project Manager agent) require a Microsoft 365 Copilot licence, with more capability for Plan 1 or Plan 3 holders. Microsoft states prompts, responses and Microsoft Graph data are not used to train foundation models, and EU traffic stays within the EU Data Boundary.

records.name: Microsoft To Do
records.blurb: Free personal task list from Microsoft with My Day, smart lists and steps, stored in Exchange Online and woven into Outlook and Teams.
summary: Microsoft To Do is a plain personal task list built by the former Wunderlist team and given away with every Microsoft account. It suits people who live in Outlook and want their own tasks, flagged email and assigned Planner tasks in one place.

Tasks sit in lists and groups, with steps, notes, due dates, reminders, recurrence and file attachments; My Day is a daily shortlist that empties each night. There is no board, calendar view, timeline, custom field or automation inside the app. Lists can be shared, but there is no assignment workflow worth the name.
There is nothing to buy. Personal accounts get everything free, and organisations get To Do with any Microsoft 365 plan that includes an Exchange Online mailbox; on-premise Exchange is not supported.

Tasks are stored in the user’s Exchange Online mailbox, so work accounts inherit Microsoft 365 encryption, certifications and tenant data location, and admins can find tasks with Purview eDiscovery. Copilot Premium users can read and edit To Do tasks through the Planner Agent since July 2026. Leaving is awkward: there is no export button, only a whole-mailbox PST from Outlook or the Graph API. Microsoft’s task investment has shifted to Planner, and from December 2026 private tasks created in Planner stop landing in To Do.
records.bandEvidence: Microsoft publishes no To Do user count; its Graph documentation (updated August 2025) says To Do reaches “millions of users”, and the app ships inside Outlook and Teams for Microsoft 365 work accounts as part of a major public company’s product line.
records.integrationNotes: Outlook tasks and flagged email, Planner assigned tasks, Teams, Microsoft Launcher, Power Automate and Zapier; the Microsoft Graph To Do API covers lists, tasks, checklist items and linked resources for personal and work accounts.
records.calendarSync: No calendar view or feed. In new Outlook and Outlook on the web, tasks can be dragged from the My Day pane onto the Outlook calendar as a time block (one-way). No Google Calendar sync.
records.dataOut: No in-app export. Personal users export the whole mailbox to PST from desktop Outlook; admins export tasks as PST via Purview content search. The Microsoft Graph To Do API reads and writes lists, tasks and checklist items. No importers.
records.caveat: Microsoft is moving task management towards Planner: Windows Latest called To Do effectively in maintenance mode in August 2026, and from December 2026 private tasks created in Planner no longer appear in To Do, though no retirement has been announced.

value.review: Entirely free with a personal Microsoft account and already paid for in most Microsoft 365 work plans.

use.review: My Day, smart lists and steps are learnt in minutes, and flagged Outlook email turns up as tasks without setup.

enterprise.review: Work accounts inherit Entra ID sign-in, licence control and Purview eDiscovery, but To Do itself has no team admin or roles.

flex.review: Lists, My Day and smart lists only: no board, calendar view, custom fields or automation inside the app.

control.review: Tasks live in the Exchange Online mailbox under Microsoft 365 certifications and tenant data location; personal accounts get no region choice.

portability.review: No export button; data leaves through an Outlook PST export, admin eDiscovery or the Graph API, and there are no importers.

sync.note: In new Outlook and Outlook on the web a task can be dragged from the My Day pane onto the Outlook calendar to book time; it is a one-way copy and Google Calendar is not supported.

commercial.vendor: Microsoft Corporation. Publicly traded (NASDAQ: MSFT), headquartered in Redmond, Washington, USA; To Do came from the team behind Wunderlist, acquired in 2015.
commercial.yearNote: 2017. Public preview released in April 2017 by the former Wunderlist team as Wunderlist’s successor.
commercial.priceNote: No paid tier of its own. Free with any personal Microsoft account (Outlook.com, Skype, Xbox); for organisations it comes with Microsoft 365 business, enterprise and education plans that include an Exchange Online mailbox.
commercial.freePlanNote: Every feature is free with a personal Microsoft account, with no list or task caps published; work and school use needs a qualifying Microsoft 365 licence with Exchange Online.
commercial.plans: Free with a personal Microsoft account; included in Microsoft 365 Family and Personal, and in Business Essentials, Business Premium, E1 to E5, F2 and Education A1 to A5 plans that carry Exchange Online.
commercial.hosting: Stored and synced in Exchange Online, so work and school data follows the Microsoft 365 tenant’s data location; personal accounts use Microsoft’s consumer cloud with no choice. No on-premise edition: on-premise Exchange mailboxes have been unsupported since March 2021.
commercial.security: Encrypted at rest on Exchange servers and in transit. Work accounts inherit Microsoft 365 compliance commitments (ISO 27001, ISO 27018, GDPR, EU Data Boundary), Entra ID sign-in with SSO and MFA, per-user licence control and Purview eDiscovery; To Do has no admin console of its own.
commercial.platforms: Web, iOS, Android, Windows and macOS, plus Outlook (web, new Outlook, mobile) and Teams. No Linux app.
commercial.ai: No AI inside the To Do app. Microsoft 365 Copilot Premium users can query and edit To Do tasks through the Planner Agent since July 2026; Microsoft states prompts, responses and Graph data are not used to train foundation models.

records.name: monday work management
records.blurb: Board-and-column work management: every project is a configurable table of items shown as table, Kanban, timeline, Gantt or calendar.
summary: monday work management is the core product of monday.com, alongside the separate CRM, dev and service products built on the same platform. It is sold to teams of any type that want to model their own process rather than adopt a fixed project method.

Everything lives on boards: rows are items, columns are typed fields such as status, people, date or formula, and the same board can be shown as a table, Kanban, timeline, Gantt chart, calendar or chart. Automations, dashboards and Workdocs connect boards together. There is no native Scrum layer in this product; sprints are sold separately in monday dev.

The free plan is for 2 seats and 3 boards, so it is a trial in practice. Every paid plan starts at 3 seats and is sold in seat buckets. Basic at $9 a seat lacks timeline, calendar, automations and integrations, so most teams need Standard at $12; time tracking, private boards, dependencies and workload sit on Pro at $19. AI runs on monthly credits (1,000 on Basic, 2,000 on Standard, 3,000 on Pro), with more available to buy.

Data is hosted on AWS in the US, Germany or Australia, with the region set by where the account is opened, and monday.com holds SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001, 27017, 27018 and 27701 certificates. SSO, SCIM, audit logs and strict EU residency are Enterprise features, and the Guardian add-on adds tenant keys and BYOK. monday.com states customer data is not used to train AI models. Boards export to Excel and the GraphQL API is complete, but Workdocs and dashboards are left out of the account export.
records.bandEvidence: monday.com reported fiscal 2025 revenue of $1,232.0 million, up 27%, with 4,281 customers above $50,000 in annual recurring revenue, per its results release of 9 February 2026.
records.integrationNotes: monday.com claims 850+ integrations and marketplace apps, including Slack, Microsoft Teams, Outlook, Gmail, Google Calendar, Salesforce, HubSpot, Jira, GitHub, Zoom and Zapier; integrations start on Standard with 250 actions a month. A public GraphQL API with webhooks is available.
records.calendarSync: Google Calendar and Outlook integration recipes from Standard. Board dates can be pushed one way, or two recipes combined so board items create events and new events create items; each run counts against the plan’s monthly integration actions.
records.dataOut: Board export to Excel with optional updates and subitems (subitem updates excluded), up to 100,000 items per board; account-wide zip of all boards with uploaded files, run by admins once every 24 hours, excluding Workdocs, dashboards and archived boards. Workdocs export separately to PDF, Word or Markdown. Public GraphQL API with webhooks; Excel, CSV and other-tool importers.
records.caveat: The 3-seat minimum and fixed seat buckets mean the bill is often higher than the per-seat price suggests: a team that falls between bucket sizes pays for the next bucket up, and exceeding a bucket auto-upgrades the plan.

value.review: A 3-seat minimum and seat buckets; timeline needs Standard at $12 and time tracking needs Pro at $19.

use.review: Colour-coded boards and templates get a team working on day one; cross-board structures take planning.

enterprise.review: SAML SSO, SCIM, audit log, multi-level permissions, portfolios and resource management, all on Enterprise only.

flex.review: More than 30 column types, many board views, dashboards across up to 50 boards, automations and an apps framework.

control.review: US, EU (Germany) or Australian hosting, strict EU residency and BYOK through the Guardian add-on on Enterprise.

portability.review: Boards export to Excel with updates; admins get a zip of all boards and files; a full GraphQL API.

The region is set automatically from the first user’s location and cannot be changed later; only EU Enterprise accounts keep all customer data, including sub-processors, inside the EU. No self-managed or on-premise edition.

commercial.ai: AI columns, AI agents, meeting notetaker and the monday vibe app builder on paid plans, metered by monthly AI credits (1,000, 2,000 and 3,000 on Basic, Standard and Pro; custom on Enterprise). monday.com states customer data is not used to train AI models, and admins can turn AI features off.

records.name: Notion
records.blurb: Workspace of pages and databases: wikis, docs and task databases shown as table, board, timeline or calendar, with AI agents built in.
summary: Notion combines documents, wikis and databases in one editor, so a project plan, its meeting notes and the task list behind it can live on the same page. It is used both by individuals and by whole companies as their internal knowledge base and planning tool.

Everything is a page made of blocks, and databases are pages whose rows are pages. A task database can be shown as a table, board, timeline with dependencies, calendar, list, gallery or chart, and linked to other databases through relations. Notion supplies templates rather than a fixed task model, so assignment, status and recurrence are whatever a team builds. There is no time tracking.

Free suits a single person; teams of two or more hit the block limit. Plus at $10 removes it. Since 13 May 2025 full Notion AI (the Notion Agent, meeting notes and enterprise search) comes only with Business at $20 and Enterprise, and Custom Agents are billed separately at $10 per 1,000 credits. Business also adds SAML SSO and private teamspaces.

Notion holds SOC 2 and ISO 27001, 27018 and 27701, and offers data residency in the US, EU, Japan or Korea on Enterprise; customer-managed keys (Enterprise Key Management) are still a beta for selected Enterprise customers. It states customer data is not used to train AI models; LLM providers keep data 30 days except on Enterprise, where retention is zero. Workspace export to Markdown, CSV and HTML with uploaded files makes leaving realistic, though relations and views do not survive.
records.bandEvidence: Notion reported passing 100 million users in August 2024 (Notion blog, 3 September 2024), and CNBC reported about $500 million in annual revenue in September 2025.
records.integrationNotes: Connections for Slack, Google Drive, GitHub, Jira, Asana, Figma, Zoom, Salesforce and Microsoft Teams, with richer synced connections on Business; Zapier and Make cover the rest. Public REST API and webhooks, plus Workers and a CLI on the 2026 developer platform.
records.calendarSync: The Notion Calendar app (macOS, Windows, iOS) connects Google and iCloud calendars and shows up to 20 Notion databases beside them, with two-way edits to dates and titles; Notion items cannot be shown inside Google, iCloud or Outlook calendars.
records.dataOut: Page or workspace export as Markdown with CSV for databases, or HTML (including comments), with uploaded files; workspace PDF and subpage PDF export on Business and Enterprise; scheduled export API in beta on Enterprise. Public REST API and webhooks; importers for Asana, Trello, Confluence, monday.com, Evernote, Google Docs, Word, CSV and Markdown.
records.caveat: Notion AI is now bundled only into Business and Enterprise, and agents are metered by credits; teams on Plus get a trial, not ongoing AI, so the real comparison price is often $20 rather than $10.

value.review: Free is generous for one person and Plus is $10, but full AI, SSO and Agents need Business at $20.

use.review: Writing a page is instant; building a working task system from blank databases takes deliberate design.

enterprise.review: SAML SSO on Business; SCIM, audit log, DLP and SIEM connections, residency and beta key management on Enterprise.

flex.review: Table, board, timeline, calendar, list, gallery, chart and form views, relations, database automations and an API.

control.review: Residency in the US, EU, Japan or Korea on Enterprise; customer-managed keys exist only as a beta for selected Enterprise customers.

portability.review: Any plan exports the whole workspace to Markdown, CSV or HTML with files; importers cover Asana, Trello and Confluence.

sync.note: Notion Calendar shows and edits database dates beside Google or iCloud events, but tasks are never written into Google or Outlook calendars and there is no iCal feed.

records.name: Smartsheet
records.blurb: Spreadsheet-style work management: sheets of rows with formulas and dependencies, shown as grid, Gantt, board or calendar, with dashboards on top.
summary: Smartsheet looks like a spreadsheet but behaves like a project tool: each row is a task with owners, dates, dependencies and attachments. It is bought mostly by large organisations and their PMOs, and by operations teams that already think in rows and columns.

A sheet can be shown as a grid, Gantt chart, board, calendar or table, and reports and dashboards roll many sheets together. Formulas, cross-sheet references, forms, approval workflows and no-code WorkApps let teams build their own systems. Much of the advanced range is sold separately: Resource Management (which holds time tracking), Dynamic View from $125 a month, Data Shuttle from $100 a month, DataMesh, Calendar App and Brandfolder.

There is no free plan. Pro at $9 suits a small team of up to 10 Members but lacks the API, timeline view and scheduled backups. Business at $19 needs 3 Members and adds those, plus unlimited automations and workload tracking. SAML SSO, portfolios and directory integration require Enterprise.

Data can sit in the US, the EU (Germany) or Australia through Smartsheet Regions, and a separate Smartsheet Gov runs on AWS GovCloud. Smartsheet lists SOC 2, ISO 27001, 27701 and 42001, with a FedRAMP Moderate authorisation for Smartsheet Gov, and says third parties never train foundation models on customer data. Backups on Business and above are Excel workbooks with comments and uploaded attachments, but formulas, reports and dashboards do not travel.
records.bandEvidence: Smartsheet’s last public results, for the quarter to 31 October 2024, showed annualised recurring revenue of $1.133 billion and 2,137 customers above $100,000 a year (SEC filing, 5 December 2024); in November 2026 it cites over 3,000 employees and use in more than 85% of Fortune 500 companies.
records.integrationNotes: Microsoft 365, Google Workspace and Slack on every plan; Power BI, Tableau, Adobe Creative Cloud and AI connectors for Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini and Copilot from Business; Workday, ServiceNow, HubSpot and Docusign on Enterprise; the pricing page counts nearly 100 more. The REST API is available from Business, not Pro.
records.calendarSync: Publish a sheet’s dates to Google Calendar (up to 600 rows, Pro and above) or as an iCal feed (Business and Enterprise), both one-way; a Google calendar can be overlaid read-only on a sheet. Changes made in the calendar do not sync back. iCal works with Outlook for Windows but not Outlook for Mac.
records.dataOut: Sheet and report export to Excel (comments on separate tabs), Google Sheets and PDF, and Gantt export to Microsoft Project XML or PNG; attachments are excluded from exports. Workspace backups as a zip of Excel workbooks with a comments tab and directly uploaded attachments (not linked files, formulas, reports or dashboards); recurring backups on Business and Enterprise. REST API from Business.
records.caveat: Smartsheet has been private since January 2025 and no longer publishes revenue; it dropped its free plan and moved to a Member and Contributor licence model, so older comparisons describe plans that no longer exist.

value.review: No free plan, Pro capped at 10 Members, Business at $19 with a 3-Member minimum, and many paid add-ons.

use.review: The grid feels like a spreadsheet, but formulas, cross-sheet references and workflows reward trained builders.

enterprise.review: SAML SSO, directory provisioning, Enterprise Plan Manager, access controls, FedRAMP for Gov, CMEK and event-reporting add-ons.

flex.review: Grid, Gantt, board, calendar, table and timeline views, dashboards, reports, forms, automations and no-code WorkApps.

control.review: US, EU (Germany) or Australian regions, a GovCloud edition and customer-managed encryption keys as an add-on.

portability.review: Sheets export to Excel with comments; scheduled backups need Business, and the API is not on Pro.

tt.note: No timer in core sheets; time and expense tracking lives in the separately priced Resource Management add-on, from Business.

sync.note: One-way in each direction: a sheet publishes to Google Calendar or any iCal client (Outlook for Windows, not Mac), and a Google calendar can be overlaid read-only on a sheet; edits do not flow back.

records.name: Trello
records.blurb: Kanban boards of lists and cards, with Power-Up add-ons; calendar, timeline and table views sit on the Premium plan.
summary: Trello is the board most people meet first: lists running left to right, cards moving between them. Atlassian sells it to any team that wants shared visual task lists without the weight of a project tool such as Jira.

Cards carry checklists, due dates, labels, attachments and custom fields, and Butler automation moves them by rule. Power-Ups add almost everything else, from Gantt charts to time tracking, which Trello does not build in. Calendar, Timeline, Table, Dashboard and Map views belong to Premium, and the Timeline has no dependencies. Planner pulls Google or Outlook events beside your cards and schedules focus time back into the calendar.

The free plan is generous on cards and Power-Ups but, since May 2024, a free Workspace with more than 10 collaborators (members, guests and pending invites) turns view-only. Standard at $5 removes the board and collaborator caps; most teams wanting more than boards will need Premium at $10.

Content is held in Atlassian’s US AWS regions, with SOC 2 and ISO 27001 coverage. AI features (board generation, checklists, smart scheduling) are on by default on paid plans. Export is JSON per board for everyone, CSV and Workspace exports with attachments for Premium, and the public API is open on all plans.
records.bandEvidence: Trello announced 50 million registered users in 2019 (VentureBeat, October 2019) and has been a product line of public company Atlassian since 2017; no newer official user count is published.
records.integrationNotes: Trello’s own guide counts upwards of 200 Power-Ups, including Slack, Google Drive, Jira, Microsoft Teams and Zapier; a public REST API with webhooks is available on every plan, plus an MCP server for AI tools.
records.calendarSync: Planner (web and desktop) connects up to 10 Google or Outlook calendar accounts, displays their events and writes focus-time blocks to them; card due dates publish one way through the Calendar Power-Up’s iCal feed.
records.dataOut: Board export as JSON on all plans (comments only within the latest 1,000 actions); CSV board export and Workspace export in JSON and CSV, optionally with raw attachments in a ZIP, need Premium. Public REST API and webhooks on all plans.
records.caveat: Since 20 May 2024, free Workspaces with more than 10 collaborators become view-only and their automations stop; no later relaxation of this limit has been announced.

value.review: A free plan for 10 collaborators and $5 Standard, but calendar, timeline and table views need $10 Premium.

use.review: Lists and cards on a board are learnt in minutes; the model has barely changed since 2011.

enterprise.review: Enterprise adds SSO and provisioning through Atlassian Guard and SOC 2 reports, but little portfolio reporting.

flex.review: Five extra views, custom fields and Butler automation exist, though most depth arrives through 200 Power-Ups.

control.review: SOC 2 and ISO 27001 under Atlassian, but content sits in US AWS regions with no residency choice.

portability.review: JSON board export on every plan is capped at 1,000 actions; CSV and full Workspace export need Premium.

gantt.note: Timeline view is Premium and Enterprise only and has no card dependencies; Gantt charts come from third-party Power-Ups.

Atlassian’s data contribution FAQ says Trello in-app data is not yet used for its August 2026 AI-training programme until settings exist for Trello.

records.name: Airtable
records.blurb: No-code relational database with a spreadsheet face: linked tables as grid, Kanban, calendar, timeline or Gantt, plus automations and AI.
summary: Airtable is a no-code database: each base holds linked tables of typed fields, and teams build their own trackers, content calendars and lightweight apps on top. It suits operations, marketing and product teams who outgrow spreadsheets but do not want a fixed project tool.

Any table can be viewed as a grid, Kanban board, calendar, gallery, form, timeline or Gantt chart, and Interfaces turn bases into custom screens for people who should not see the raw data. Automations, scripting and the Omni AI assistant sit across the whole base. It is not a task manager out of the box: assignment, recurrence and time tracking have to be modelled.

Free allows 5 editors and 1,000 records a base, which suits a trial or a small project. Team at $20 a seat raises that to 50,000 records with Gantt and timeline views; Business at $45 adds SSO, the admin panel and two-way sync between bases. AI runs on monthly credits (15,000 per seat on Team), with top-ups from $20 per 10,000.

Airtable holds SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001 and 27701 certificates. Data residency in the US, Europe or Australia and customer-managed keys are Enterprise Scale features, and its AI terms bar Airtable and its model providers from training on customer data. Export is CSV per view, so a full exit means using the API. Bending Spoons completed its purchase of Airtable on 4 September 2026 and let go a large part of the pre-acquisition team in October; it says nothing changes for customers’ plans or prices.
records.bandEvidence: Bending Spoons agreed in August 2026 to buy Airtable at an enterprise value of $1.285 billion, citing annual recurring revenue of about $480 million in June 2026 (SEC 6-K, 4 August 2026); Airtable’s about page cites 500,000 companies and 10 million active users (November 2026).
records.integrationNotes: Native sync and automation connectors for Slack, Gmail, Google Drive, Google Calendar, Outlook, Salesforce, Jira, GitHub, Zendesk, Box, Snowflake, Databricks and Tableau, plus Marketplace extensions and an MCP server for Claude and ChatGPT. Public REST API with webhooks on every plan, capped at 1,000 calls a month on Free.
records.calendarSync: One-way iCal subscription from a shared calendar view on all plans (external apps refresh on their own schedule, up to 24 hours). Google Calendar and Outlook Calendar sync integrations bring events into a table one way on paid plans; updating events from Airtable needs an automation.
records.dataOut: CSV download per view (attachments as URLs; comments not included); XLSX and PDF only by converting the CSV. Snapshots restore a base inside Airtable. Public REST API and webhooks API on all plans; importers for CSV, Excel, Google Sheets and Smartsheet exports.
records.caveat: Bending Spoons completed its $1.285 billion acquisition on 4 September 2026 and parted with a large share of the pre-acquisition team in October; it says plans, prices and service are unchanged, so check terms at renewal.

value.review: A free plan for 5 editors and 1,000 records a base, then $20 a seat, and $45 for SSO and admin.

use.review: The grid is familiar at once, but linked tables, interfaces and automations ask for database thinking.

enterprise.review: SAML SSO and admin panel on Business; audit logs, EKM, residency and org units on Enterprise Scale.

flex.review: Grid, Kanban, calendar, gallery, form, list, timeline and Gantt views, interfaces, automations, scripting and extensions.

control.review: US, EU or Australian residency and customer-owned AWS KMS keys, both on Enterprise Scale only.

portability.review: CSV per view only, without comments; the full REST API and webhooks are the real exit.

tt.note: Only the vendor’s Time tracker extension, a start-stop timer that writes to a duration field, on paid plans; no timesheets or time reports.

sync.note: One-way each direction: an iCal feed out of a calendar view, and Google or Outlook Calendar sync into a table; events can be updated back only by building automations.

Airtable’s AI terms state neither Airtable nor its providers train on customer data; providers may keep inputs up to 30 days for abuse monitoring on Free and Team.

records.name: Any.do
records.blurb: Personal to-do list and daily planner with a mirrored calendar and WhatsApp reminders, plus Family and Teams boards with Kanban and Gantt views.
summary: Any.do is a to-do list and daily planner that puts tasks next to the events of your existing calendar, with reminders that can arrive on WhatsApp. It is aimed at individuals and households first, with a Teams plan for small groups who want shared boards.

Personal plans offer lists, subtasks, My Day and a calendar view that mirrors Google, Outlook or iCloud events. Family adds shared boards and a grocery list. Teams adds Kanban, table, calendar and Gantt views, custom fields, task chat, rule automations and time tracking, though the help centre documents few details of the last two.

The free plan has no task cap but holds back recurring tasks, WhatsApp reminders, tags and AI. Premium is $4.99 a month billed annually, and Teams is the same per member with no stated minimum, which makes it one of the cheaper shared boards. Importers from Trello, Asana, ClickUp, Monday and Todoist need Family or Teams.

Data protection is thinly documented: the vendor names no hosting provider, region or certification, and states encryption in transit only. An MCP server lets ChatGPT and Claude read and edit tasks on every plan. Leaving is easier from boards, which export to CSV or Excel, than from personal lists, which print to PDF or export archived tasks as CSV.
records.bandEvidence: Any.do’s homepage claims 50M+ people and 651K app-store reviews averaging 4.8 (checked November 2026); no revenue or headcount is published.
records.integrationNotes: Google, Outlook and iCloud calendars, WhatsApp, Gmail, Slack, Zoom, Siri and Apple Reminders, Zapier, Make, Pabbly and Integrately; an MCP server for ChatGPT and Claude, but no documented public REST API or webhooks.
records.calendarSync: Google, Outlook or iCloud (one account) on web and desktop, and device calendars on iOS and Android, mirrored into the calendar view on all plans. The help centre says events can be added, edited and deleted from Any.do with invitations sent through the native provider, while a 2026 Any.do blog post says the sync is read-based for events and that tasks reach Google Calendar only when scheduled as time blocks. No documented route for calendar edits to update a task.
records.dataOut: Boards export to CSV, Excel or PDF on Family and Teams; personal lists print to PDF, and archived personal tasks export as CSV by email. Comments and attachments are not documented as included. No public REST API; an MCP server with OAuth. Importers from Trello, Asana, ClickUp, Monday and Todoist on Family and Teams.
records.caveat: Any.do publishes no hosting location, security certification or AI training policy beyond Google API data, so organisations with compliance needs have little to check.

value.review: Unlimited tasks free, then $4.99 a month for Premium or per Teams member, with no seat minimum.

use.review: Lists, My Day and a calendar beside them are clear within minutes; boards and automations only appear on Family and Teams.

enterprise.review: Teams has admin tools and permissions, but no SSO, audit log, certifications or published security documentation.

flex.review: Teams adds Kanban, table, calendar and Gantt views, custom fields and rule automations; personal plans stay list and calendar only.

control.review: No hosting provider, region or certification is published, and only encryption in transit is stated.

portability.review: Boards export to CSV or Excel on Family and Teams, but personal lists print only to PDF; no REST API.

tt.note: Time tracking is listed only for the Teams plan, and the help centre documents no timesheets or time reports.

gantt.note: A Gantt view is listed only on the Teams plan, and task dependencies are not documented.

sync.note: Google, Outlook and iCloud events are mirrored into Any.do on all plans; tasks reach Google Calendar only when scheduled as time blocks, and no edit-back from the external calendar to the task is documented. Any.do’s own pages disagree on whether event access is read-only.

commercial.ai: AI features on Premium and above, plus a beta MCP connector for ChatGPT, Claude and other agents on all plans. The privacy policy’s no-training commitment is stated for Google Workspace API data only; no AI provider is named.

records.name: Basecamp
records.blurb: Project workspace for small teams and client work: to-dos, message boards, Kanban card tables, chat, docs and a calendar per project.
summary: Basecamp organises work as projects, each a page of tools: a message board, to-do lists, a Kanban card table, group chat, docs and files, and scheduled check-ins. It is built for small companies, agencies and anyone who invites clients into the work.

Basecamp 5, released in 2026, added subtasks, a global calendar, account-wide Everything pages and Markdown in documents. Planning stays deliberately light: hill charts show progress by feel, and Lineup places whole projects on a 13-week timeline. There are no custom fields, automations, dependencies or dashboards, and time tracking is a manual timesheet.

Pricing is a flat monthly fee for the account rather than per seat. Freelancer at $29 covers five users and three active projects; Pro at $79 and Pro Plus at $99 raise those to 10 and 15 users. Pro Unlimited, $199 a month billed annually, removes the caps and is the only package with annual billing and the Admin Pro Pack. Large teams pay little per head; a seven-person team with ten live projects already needs Pro Plus.

Data sits on 37signals’ own servers in the United States after its 2023 exit from the public cloud, with no residency choice and no SOC 2 or ISO 27001 certificate. There are no built-in AI features, and the privacy policy says content is not used to train models. Leaving means an HTML archive of every project plus files, or the public API.
records.bandEvidence: Basecamp’s homepage (November 2026) claims 84 million accounts and 60 million projects created to date, and says nearly a million people and organisations rely on it daily.
records.integrationNotes: The integrations directory lists roughly 100 third-party tools, mostly time trackers (Harvest, Clockify, Everhour), Zapier, Zoho Flow and Unito; there is a public REST API with webhooks, official SDKs, a CLI and an MCP connector for ChatGPT and Claude.
records.calendarSync: One-way iCal subscription of the global or a project calendar (events, or events plus assignments) into Google, Apple, Outlook or HEY; updates can take a few hours. All plans.
records.dataOut: Account owners can export the whole account, selected projects or Ping conversations as an HTML archive including files and comments; timesheets export as CSV; full REST API with webhooks, SDKs and a CLI. The HTML export cannot be re-imported.
records.caveat: Basecamp’s packages changed during 2026 and its help centre still names plans (Studio, Unlimited) that no longer appear on the pricing page; only Pro Unlimited can be billed annually.

value.review: Flat pricing from $29 a month for five users gets cheap per head, but project caps and a one-project free plan bite.

use.review: Every project is the same toolbox of messages, to-dos, cards and chat, so new people and clients orient in minutes.

enterprise.review: The vendor states it supports no SSO or SAML, no SCIM, and only the top package adds permission restrictions and enforced 2FA.

flex.review: Lists, card tables, a calendar and hill charts, but no custom fields, automations or dashboards.

control.review: Runs on 37signals’ own hardware in the United States, with no SOC 2 or ISO 27001, only self-assessed questionnaires.

portability.review: An owner-only HTML export with files covers every project and the API is complete, but tasks never export as CSV or JSON.

tt.note: Timesheets with CSV reports exist only on Pro Plus and Pro Unlimited, and hours are logged manually without a running timer.

gantt.note: Lineup shows whole projects as bars on a rolling 13-week timeline; there are no task-level bars or dependencies.

sync.note: One-way iCal subscription to Google, Apple, Outlook or HEY calendars; changes made outside Basecamp do not flow back.

commercial.vendor: 37signals LLC. Privately held and self-funded, based in Chicago, United States; also makes HEY and Fizzy.
commercial.yearNote: 2004. Public launch of Basecamp by 37signals in 2004; the current version, Basecamp 5, shipped in 2026.
commercial.priceNote: Flat rate, not per user: Freelancer is $29 a month for the whole account (up to 5 users, 3 active projects), billed monthly only; annual billing exists only on Pro Unlimited ($199 a month billed annually, $329 monthly).
commercial.priceDagger: Flat rate, not per user: Freelancer is $29 a month for the whole account (up to 5 users, 3 active projects), billed monthly only; annual billing exists only on Pro Unlimited ($199 a month billed annually, $329 monthly). Shown as $7.90 a person: the cost for a ten-person team.
commercial.freePlanNote: Basecamp Personal is free for one project, three users and 1 GB of storage, without templates, time tracking or multiple tools per project.
commercial.plans: Basecamp Personal, free (1 project, 3 users); Freelancer $29/month (3 active projects, 5 users, 10 GB); Pro $79/month (8 projects, 10 users, 25 GB); Pro Plus $99/month (12 projects, 15 users, 100 GB, time tracking); Pro Unlimited $199/month billed annually or $329 monthly (unlimited projects and users, 1 TB, Admin Pro Pack).
commercial.hosting: 37signals’ own servers in colocation facilities, primarily in the United States; no EU or other region choice and no self-managed edition.
commercial.security: No SOC 2 or ISO 27001; PCI DSS SAQ A self-assessment, published CSA CAIQ v4.1 and HECVAT 4 questionnaires, DPA on request. No SSO, SAML or SCIM; Google sign-in and 2FA available, with enforced 2FA and permission restrictions in the Admin Pro Pack on Pro Unlimited.
commercial.platforms: Web; iOS and Android apps; desktop apps for macOS and Windows; installable PWA in Chrome (including Linux), Safari and Edge.
commercial.ai: No built-in AI features process customer content. Users can connect their own agents through the CLI or the ChatGPT and Claude MCP connectors on all plans; 37signals says content is not used to train AI models.

records.name: Bitrix24
records.blurb: A business suite whose tasks module offers lists, Kanban, Gantt, Scrum and time tracking beside CRM, chat and documents. Cloud or self-hosted.
summary: Bitrix24 is a business suite in which tasks and projects share a workspace with CRM, chat, video calls, documents, sites and HR tools. It is sold to small and mid-sized organisations that want one vendor for most of their software.

The tasks module offers list, Kanban, planner, calendar and Gantt views with four dependency types, plus subtasks, checklists, templates, recurring tasks and automation rules. Scrum boards, full time tracking and workload reports arrive on Professional. The breadth is also the cost: the task manager is one item in a long menu, and the interface carries every other module with it.

Pricing is a flat monthly fee per organisation. The free plan has no user cap but stops at 5 GB and one admin. Standard at $99 a month (annual) covers 50 users; Professional at $199 covers 100. Since 1 September 2026 each plan has a cheaper Essentials version without REST API, MCP server or unlimited AI, and a Vibe+ version with them; monthly and quarterly customers move to Essentials limits on 30 November 2026, annual ones at their next renewal.
