Data sits on AWS in the EU under a SOC 2 Type II report and a DPA with Standard Contractual Clauses. AI runs on OpenAI, Anthropic and Google models, with a stated commitment that neither Productive nor its providers train on customer data. Exports are per table, so leaving at scale means the API.
records.bandEvidence: Productive reports 2,000+ customer companies in 65+ countries and 150+ employees (productive.io, about page, November 2026).
records.integrationNotes: 24 marketplace integrations, mostly accounting (QuickBooks, Xero, Exact, Sage) and HR (BambooHR, Personio, HiBob), plus Jira, HubSpot, Salesforce, Slack, Teams and Zapier; a public API on every plan, webhooks on Ultimate, and an MCP server.
records.calendarSync: Google Calendar and Outlook events show (one way) in the My Time calendar to be converted into time entries; tasks and resourcing schedules publish out through iCal links to Google, Outlook or Apple Calendar; absence status syncs to Google Calendar.
records.dataOut: Any table exports to CSV, XLS or PDF, up to 3,000 rows per export; the Gantt layout exports separately. Public API on every plan, webhooks on Ultimate; data import tools and a sandbox. Productive says it will provide all your data on request.
records.caveat: The Gantt layout and saved views sit on Professional, so a team that needs scheduling pays $25, not $10, per seat.

value.review: Essential’s $10 includes budgets, time tracking and the API, but Gantt, approvals and rate cards need Professional at $25.

use.review: Budgets, services, rate cards and bookings must be set up before projects and timesheets mean anything.

enterprise.review: SAML SSO on every plan, SCIM for Entra and Okta, SOC 2 Type II; enforced SSO and webhooks only on Ultimate.

flex.review: List, board, table, calendar, Gantt and workload layouts, custom fields, dashboards, automations and configurable AI agents.

control.review: SOC 2 Type II and a DPA with SCCs, but hosting is AWS in the EU only, with no region choice.

portability.review: Tables export to CSV, XLS or PDF in 3,000-row batches; the full API is the only bulk route out.

sync.note: Google and Outlook events flow one way into My Time for logging; tasks and schedules flow out only as iCal links.

commercial.vendor: The Productive Company, Inc. Self-funded and profitable; incorporated in Delaware, US, with its office and hiring in Zagreb, Croatia; founded by the people who built a 350-person design and development firm.
commercial.yearNote: 2014. Launch year implied by the vendor’s “12 years” of building Productive, stated in November 2026.
commercial.priceNote: Essential, per user per month billed annually; $12 billed monthly; minimum 3 seats.
commercial.priceDagger: Essential, per user per month billed annually; $12 billed monthly; minimum 3 seats.
commercial.freePlanNote: No free plan; a 14-day trial needs no credit card.
commercial.plans: Essential $10 and Professional $25 per user per month billed annually ($12 and $29 monthly), minimum 3 seats; Ultimate by quote; the AI Notetaker is a paid add-on.
commercial.hosting: Amazon Web Services in the EU, with real-time backups (5-minute recovery point) and a standby replica. No region choice and no self-managed edition.
commercial.security: SOC 2 Type II (report on request); GDPR and CCPA policies, a DPA with Standard Contractual Clauses and a published sub-processor list. SAML 2.0 SSO (Google Workspace, Okta, Microsoft Entra) on all plans, SCIM provisioning for Entra and Okta, enforced SSO or 2FA on Ultimate.
commercial.platforms: Web; desktop and mobile apps for time tracking and work; Slack and Microsoft Teams apps.
commercial.ai: AI assistant, AI time tracking, report generation, search, agents, skills, connectors and an MCP server, with a monthly usage allowance on every plan and paid top-ups; the Notetaker is an add-on. Models come from OpenAI, Anthropic and Google, admins can restrict them, and Productive states customer data is not used for training.

records.name: Quire
records.blurb: Infinitely nested task lists with Kanban, timeline, calendar, table and dashboard views over the same tree.
summary: Quire is built around one idea: a task list that nests without limit, so a project breaks down into subtasks of subtasks and every other view reads from that tree. It is aimed at small teams and planners who think in outlines rather than boards.

The same tasks appear as a nested list, a Kanban board, a timeline with finish-to-start dependencies, a calendar, a table, dashboards and insight charts. Sublists and smart folders slice work across projects, and collaborative documents sit beside the tasks. Time tracking, a Pomodoro timer and time reports arrive with Professional; timesheets and approvals with Premium.

The free plan covers 10 members and 4 projects but stops at the list and board. Professional at $7.65 a member opens the timeline, calendar, table and time tracking, which is the tier most teams will need; Premium at $13.95 adds two-way Google Calendar sync. External guests count as paid members.

Data is held on AWS in the United States under an ISO 27001:2022 certificate, and the privacy policy says it is processed in the US and Taiwan. Quire has no built-in AI assistant; instead an MCP server and CLI let outside AI tools read and write tasks. Exports in CSV and JSON plus a public API make leaving practical.
records.bandEvidence: Quire’s about page cites 51,000+ teams in 191 countries and 3.5 million tasks completed in 2025, while its homepage claims over 100,000 teams (both read November 2026); no revenue or headcount is published.
records.integrationNotes: The App Directory lists at least 30 entries, including Google Calendar sync, Slack, GitHub, Zapier, Dropbox, Box, Gmail and Outlook add-ins and connectors for Claude, ChatGPT and Copilot via Quire MCP. A public REST API is on every plan, rate-limited by tier.
records.calendarSync: Free and Professional: one-way sync from Quire to Google Calendar (Professional adds Instant Sync). Premium and Enterprise: two-way Google Calendar sync and Google-to-Quire import. Apple Calendar sync is listed in the App Directory.
records.dataOut: Per-project export to CSV or JSON on all plans; organisation-wide export of every project on paid plans. The API’s export endpoints (Professional and up) return JSON covering tasks, users, tags, sublists, documents, chats and dashboards, and CSV that can include text comments; attachments are not part of either. Imports: CSV, JSON from Asana, Trello and Todoist, and clipboard. Public REST API on all plans.
records.caveat: Free-plan users get neither timeline nor calendar view, and external collaborators are billed as full members on paid plans.

value.review: A free plan for 10 members and 4 projects, then $7.65 a member; two-way calendar sync needs $13.95 Premium.

use.review: The nested list is quick to start with, though sublists, smart folders and views take some learning.

enterprise.review: SAML SSO and IP allowlisting on Enterprise only; no SCIM or audit log is published.

flex.review: Nine views over one task tree plus custom fields, formulas, dashboards and approvals, but no rule-based automation.

control.review: ISO 27001:2022 certified, but all data sits on AWS in the United States with no region choice.

portability.review: CSV and JSON export on every plan, comments via the API export, importers for Asana, Trello and Todoist; attachments stay behind.

commercial.vendor: Potix Corporation. Privately held software company headquartered in Taipei, Taiwan; its terms are governed by Taiwan law.
commercial.yearNote: 2014. First public release in August 2014, per Quire’s own FAQ.
commercial.priceNote: Professional, per member per month billed annually; $10.95 billed monthly. External team members count as paid members.
commercial.freePlanNote: Up to 10 members and 4 projects with nested lists, Kanban, one custom field, 3MB files and 400MB storage (100MB of uploads, per the small print); no timeline, calendar view or time tracking.
commercial.plans: Free $0; Professional $7.65 per member per month yearly ($10.95 monthly); Premium $13.95 ($18.95 monthly); Enterprise $19.95 ($24.95 monthly), with custom terms on request.
commercial.hosting: Amazon Web Services in the United States; the privacy policy says data is stored and processed in the US and Taiwan. No region choice, no self-managed edition.
commercial.security: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 certified; TLS for all traffic; continuous off-site backups. SAML SSO, Microsoft Entra External ID and IP allowlisting on Enterprise. No SOC 2, SCIM or audit log published.
commercial.platforms: Web, iOS, Android (Play Store or APK), a Quire Desktop app, a Chrome extension, and Gmail and Outlook add-ins.
commercial.ai: No built-in AI features. Quire MCP and a CLI connect external assistants such as Claude, ChatGPT, Copilot, Cursor and Gemini CLI; their data handling follows those tools’ terms.

records.name: Redbooth
records.blurb: Team task manager with workspaces, Kanban boards, a Gantt timeline, a team calendar and Zoom calls inside tasks. Free for two users.
summary: Redbooth is a long-running team task manager, launched as Teambox in Barcelona and renamed in 2014. It is aimed at small and mid-sized teams such as agencies, construction firms and higher-education marketing groups that want tasks, discussion and video calls in one place.

Work sits in workspaces holding task lists, conversations, notes and files. Tasks can be viewed on a Kanban board, a timeline with finish-to-start dependencies, a team calendar or a cross-workspace overview, and Zoom-powered HD meetings start from a task. Workspace templates, web forms and public links (added in October 2026) round it out; custom fields and built-in automation rules are not documented.

The free plan stops at two users and two workspaces. Pro at $9 per user per month (annual) adds dependencies, time tracking, SAML SSO, video calls and the MCP server; Business at $15 adds reports, swimlanes, time estimates and Redbooth AI, which trims titles, suggests subtasks and summarises comment threads.

Data is on AWS in a region the vendor does not name, with no residency choice; the security page still cites Privacy Shield, and neither the terms nor the DPA names a legal entity. The AI provider and training policy are not stated. Leaving is realistic: admins can generate a ZIP of JSON files with every task, comment and conversation.
records.bandEvidence: Redbooth’s about page (read November 2026) says 3,000 companies use it every day; in January 2013 Teambox reported more than 1,700 paying companies.
records.integrationNotes: Box, Google Drive, Dropbox, OneDrive for Business, Okta, Slack, Webex, Zoom, Gmail and Outlook add-ins, a Chrome extension, Hubstaff, Clockify, Paydirt, TestLodge and Zapier; an OAuth REST API and an MCP server on Pro and Business.
records.calendarSync: One-way iCal subscription per project or for all projects, showing all tasks or only yours, into Google, Outlook, Yahoo or Apple calendars; updates can take up to 24 hours. No two-way sync.
records.dataOut: Organisation admins can export a ZIP of JSON files with all tasks including comments, task lists, conversations, notes, file links and workspaces; users can export their own data; Pro and Business can export all tasks to a spreadsheet (comments from the last 30 days); OAuth REST API; Gantt export.
records.caveat: Redbooth is still sold and updated (web forms and public links in October 2026; iOS app 8.81 on 20 October 2026), but its terms and DPA name no legal entity or governing law, and its security page still relies on the Privacy Shield framework invalidated in 2020, with a sentence naming another company, Notion Inc.

value.review: Free stops at two users; Pro at $9 a user adds dependencies, time tracking and SSO without a seat minimum.

use.review: Workspaces, task lists and a board view that a new team can use the same day.

enterprise.review: SAML SSO from Pro and multi-organisation settings on Enterprise, but no SCIM, audit log or certification of its own.

flex.review: Kanban, timeline, calendar and overview views with templates, web forms and reports; no custom fields or automation rules documented.

control.review: AWS hosting in an unnamed region with no residency choice, and a security page still citing Privacy Shield.

portability.review: Admins download every task, comment and conversation as JSON, plus an OAuth API, but importers are copy and paste.

sync.note: One-way iCal subscription of all or only your tasks into Google, Outlook or Apple calendars, which can take up to 24 hours to update.

commercial.vendor: Redbooth, Inc. (the seller named on its App Store listing; formerly Teambox), headquartered in Auburn, California, USA, with staff in Toronto, Barcelona, Paris and Thailand. Privately held and venture-backed (Avalon Ventures, NHN Ventures, Andreessen, Y Combinator per its about page); its terms and DPA name only “Redbooth”, with no legal entity, address or governing law.
commercial.yearNote: 2008. Founding of Teambox in Barcelona in 2008; the product was relaunched under the Redbooth name in January 2014.
commercial.priceNote: Pro, per user per month billed annually; $12 billed monthly. No seat minimum is stated.
commercial.freePlanNote: Up to 2 users and 2 workspaces with Kanban, timeline, calendar and 2 GB storage; no dependencies, time tracking, SSO or video calls.
commercial.plans: Free (2 users); Pro $9 per user per month billed annually ($12 monthly); Business $15 ($18.75) with reports, swimlanes, time estimates and Redbooth AI; Enterprise quote-only with 500 GB storage and multi-organisation settings.
commercial.hosting: Amazon Web Services (S3 for files, RDS MySQL in a virtual private cloud); the region is not stated and there is no residency choice or self-managed edition.
commercial.security: TLS 1.2, hashed and salted passwords, penetration testing; ISO 27001, PCI DSS Level 1 and SAS70 cited for the AWS data centre rather than Redbooth itself; SAML SSO (Okta, OneLogin, Shibboleth) on Pro and above; no SCIM or customer audit log documented. The security page still claims EU-U.S. and Swiss-U.S. Privacy Shield compliance (struck down in 2020) and its certification sentence names “Notion Inc.”; the DPA covers GDPR and CCPA but names no transfer mechanism.
commercial.platforms: Web, iOS and Android, plus a Chrome extension and Gmail and Outlook add-ins.
commercial.ai: Redbooth AI (title trimming, subtask suggestions, comment summaries) on Business and Enterprise since June 2025; the MCP server for Claude and other assistants on Pro and Business. The AI provider and any training policy are not stated.

records.name: Shortcut
records.blurb: Agile tracker for product and engineering teams: stories, epics, iterations and objectives on Kanban boards, with docs and reports built in.
summary: Shortcut, called Clubhouse until 2021, organises software work as stories grouped into epics, timed into iterations and tied to objectives. It is sold to product and engineering teams that want sprints and a roadmap without Jira’s administration.

Stories move across Kanban boards through custom workflows; a backlog, a roadmap with table and timeline layouts, built-in docs and reports for velocity, cycle time and cumulative flow sit alongside. The roadmap timeline draws no dependencies, there is no calendar view and no time tracking. Korey, an AI agent launched in September 2025, drafts specs and stories and hands work to coding agents.

The free plan covers 10 users with one team and one workflow. Team at $8.50 a seat (yearly) adds automations, WIP limits, five workflows and the calendar feed; Business at $12 adds unlimited teams, objectives and key results, advanced custom fields and extra workspaces. SSO costs extra until Enterprise.

Data sits on AWS with SOC 2 Type II audits and backups every 10 minutes; there is no region choice. Korey is priced per organisation, and Shortcut says Korey inputs and outputs are not used for training. Leaving means CSV story exports or the API, with importers in from Jira, Trello, Linear and Pivotal Tracker.
records.bandEvidence: Shortcut says it is trusted by thousands of software teams (shortcut.com, November 2026); it raised about $39 million to its $25 million Series B in January 2020 and has around 80 employees (Wikipedia, 2026).
records.integrationNotes: The help-centre directory lists about 85 integrations, including GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, Slack, Figma, Sentry, Zendesk, Zapier and coding agents through the hosted MCP server; a public REST API and outgoing webhooks on every plan.
records.calendarSync: Paid plans only: one-way public iCal feeds of due dates for your stories, the whole workspace, workflows, epics and objectives, for Google Calendar, Outlook or Apple Calendar; Google may take up to 12 hours to refresh, and nothing flows back.
records.dataOut: CSV export of stories from a workspace, iteration, epic, label or space, including name, description, owners, labels, tasks and dates but not comments or attachments. REST API and outgoing webhooks; importers for Jira, Trello, Linear (with comments and files), Pivotal Tracker and CSV.
records.caveat: SSO is a paid add-on below Enterprise and the AI agent Korey carries its own per-organisation subscription, so the per-seat price understates the cost for teams that want both.

value.review: Ten free users with sprints and a roadmap, then $8.50 a seat; custom fields and objectives wait for $12 Business.

use.review: Stories, epics and iterations map directly onto how software teams already talk, and the board needs little setup.

enterprise.review: SAML and Okta-only SCIM are add-ons below Enterprise, there is no customer-facing audit log, and SOC 2 reports are by request.

flex.review: Boards, backlog, roadmap table and timeline, docs, burndown and cycle-time reports and custom workflows, but no calendar view.

control.review: SOC 2 Type II and a HIPAA BAA, but one AWS hosting location with no residency choice and no self-managed edition.

portability.review: Story CSVs leave out comments, but the REST API is open on every plan and importers cover Jira, Trello, Linear and Pivotal.

gantt.note: The Roadmap timeline plots dated epics but draws no dependencies; blocked and blocking stories appear only in a separate chart on epic and iteration pages.

sync.note: One-way iCal feeds of story, epic and objective due dates, on paid plans only.

commercial.vendor: Shortcut Software Company. Privately held, venture-backed (Battery Ventures, Greylock Partners); founded in New York City in 2014, headquartered there.
commercial.yearNote: 2016. Public launch as Clubhouse in 2016 after a year in beta; renamed Shortcut on 13 September 2021.
commercial.priceNote: Team, per user per month billed annually; $10 billed monthly.
commercial.freePlanNote: Up to 10 users, one team, one workspace, one workflow and 5 GB of storage, with boards, roadmap, iterations, docs and basic reports; no calendar feed or automations.
commercial.plans: Free $0 for up to 10 users; Team $8.50 per user per month yearly ($10 monthly); Business $12 yearly ($16 monthly); Enterprise custom pricing. SAML SSO and SCIM are paid add-ons on Business and included on Enterprise; the Korey AI agent is billed separately from $99 per organisation per month.
commercial.hosting: Amazon Web Services; the security page names no region and offers no data residency choice. No self-managed or on-premise edition.
commercial.security: SOC 2 Type II (security, availability, confidentiality), reports available by request; a HIPAA BAA by request, which the security page offers on Business and Enterprise but the pricing table lists for Enterprise only; encrypted backups every 10 minutes. Google SSO on all plans; SAML SSO and SCIM (Okta only) are add-ons on Business and included on Enterprise; no customer-facing audit log is listed.
commercial.platforms: Web application. No Shortcut app turned up in an Apple App Store search in November 2026, and neither the help centre nor the pricing page documents a mobile or desktop app; the iOS app announced in 2019 appears to be gone.
commercial.ai: Korey (launched September 2025) drafts specs, breaks them into stories, answers status questions and prepares work for coding agents; billed separately with 100 free interactions, then from $99 per organisation per month. Korey’s privacy policy says inputs and outputs are not used to train its models and its model providers are bound likewise. An MCP server is available on all plans.

records.name: Sunsama
records.blurb: A daily planner that pulls tasks from email, calendars and work tools into a day-by-day board, with timeboxing on your real calendar.
summary: Sunsama is a daily planner for knowledge workers who want each morning to start with a deliberate plan. It is sold per person, with a shared-workspace option for teams who want one bill.

The core object is a task placed on a day. A board of day columns sits beside your real calendar, and you drag tasks into time slots that write back to Google, Outlook or iCloud. Integrations pull issues, cards and emails in from Jira, Asana, Linear, Gmail and about 20 other tools. There are channels, weekly objectives and a timer, but no projects in the usual sense, no custom fields and no Gantt.

There is one self-serve plan, Pro, at $17 a month billed annually or $22 monthly, and no free tier. That single plan replaced a short-lived split into Basic Pro and Power Pro in spring 2026, and it still makes Sunsama one of the dearest per-seat tools in this comparison for a single person.

All data is stored in the United States on Google Cloud, MongoDB Atlas and AWS. SOC 2 Type II arrived in late 2025, and SSO, SCIM and audit logs sit on a quote-only Enterprise tier. The AI assistant, Sunny, and the MCP server are on Pro, and the privacy policy says customer data never trains models. Leaving relies on a whole-history export, since there is no public API.
records.bandEvidence: No user count is published (the ‘300k+’ on its site counts newsletter readers); third-party profiles cite over 10,000 paying users and Latka estimates about $1.1M revenue for 2023, both unverified.
records.integrationNotes: Google, Outlook, iCloud and CalDAV calendars; Gmail and Outlook mail; Asana, ClickUp, GitHub, Jira, Linear, Monday.com, Notion, Todoist, Trello, Microsoft Planner and To Do, Slack, Teams, Toggl and Zapier. No public REST API or webhooks; a hosted MCP server is the only official programmatic route.
records.calendarSync: Two-way with Google, Outlook, iCloud and CalDAV (including Fastmail and Nextcloud) on Pro: events show in Sunsama, edits and timeboxed tasks write back to the source calendar.
records.dataOut: Whole-history export from account settings (JSON per the security page); export data gained backlog and daily priority in October 2026, and users report subtasks are missing. No public REST API or webhooks; a hosted MCP server and Zapier can read and write tasks.
records.caveat: Pricing has changed three times in a year: $16 annually or $20 monthly in late 2025, Basic Pro at $20/$25 and Power Pro at $50/$65 by February 2026, then one Pro plan at $17/$22 by May 2026. The pricing FAQ kept quoting $20/$25 until late October 2026, which is where older third-party figures come from.

value.review: No free plan and $17 to $22 a month per person, more than most team tools charge for a single seat.

use.review: A guided morning planning ritual and drag-to-calendar timeboxing; productive on day one if your work already lives in connected tools.

enterprise.review: SOC 2 Type II and SSO through WorkOS, but only on a quote-only Enterprise tier, with a thin billing-only admin role.

flex.review: Day board, calendar panel, weekly objectives and channels, with an AI assistant; no custom fields, statuses or automation rules.

control.review: SOC 2 Type II and a GDPR DPA, but all data stays in the United States with no EU residency option.

portability.review: A full-history export exists, but there is no public API; only an MCP server and Zapier reach the data.

agile.note: The main view is a Kanban board, but its columns are days, not custom statuses.

commercial.vendor: Summay, Inc., a Delaware corporation with a business address in Alexandria, Virginia, US. Privately held and fully remote; Y Combinator backed in 2018, $2.4M seed, profitable since 2022.
commercial.yearNote: 2018. Public launch on Product Hunt, as the vendor’s About page records it.
commercial.priceNote: Pro, per person per month billed annually ($204 a year); $22 billed monthly. Each teammate in a shared workspace costs the same.
commercial.freePlanNote: No free plan, and the vendor says it does not intend one; a 14-day trial with every feature and no card required.
commercial.plans: Pro at $17 per person per month billed annually or $22 monthly, with unlimited integrations, AI, MCP and Zapier; Enterprise is quote-only and adds SSO/SAML, SCIM, audit logs and custom privacy terms.
commercial.hosting: Google Cloud Platform with MongoDB Atlas and AWS; ‘All data is stored in the United States.’ No EU residency, though the vendor says it could be considered for enterprise clients. No self-managed edition.
commercial.security: SOC 2 Type I (September 2025) and Type II, report on request; ISO 27001 principles followed but not certified. TLS 1.2+ in transit and AES-256 at rest. SSO/SAML via WorkOS, SCIM and audit logs on Enterprise only.
commercial.platforms: Web, macOS, Windows, Linux, iOS and Android; the mobile apps are companions to the desktop planner.
commercial.ai: Sunny, a chat and voice assistant that creates and plans tasks, reads connected accounts and logs time, plus an OAuth MCP server for ChatGPT and Claude, both on Pro and out of beta in 2026. The privacy policy (updated 30 September 2026) says user data is never used to train models, including by third-party AI providers.

records.name: Superlist
records.blurb: A to-do list app from the Wunderlist team: lists that double as documents, shared with others, with AI voice capture and meeting notes.
summary: Superlist is a to-do list app from the people who built Wunderlist, rebuilt after Microsoft closed that app. It is aimed at individuals and small groups who share household or project lists, with AI capture added on top.

A list is a document: tasks sit beside text, headers and images, and each task opens into its own page of subtasks, notes and attachments. Lists can be shared with assignees and comments. Meeting notes and voice input turn speech into tasks. There is no board, calendar view, time tracking or Gantt.

The free plan stops at five private and five shared lists. Basic, at $59 a year or $6 a month, removes those limits and opens the integrations, while Super at $249 a year is for heavy AI meeting-note use. Teams pay the same per-member rate.

The privacy policy names Hetzner in Germany for hosting, alongside US processors, and Google Gemini, OpenAI and Deepgram for AI features; it does not say whether those providers may train on your data. A CSV export of the whole account arrived in January 2026, and an MCP server in May 2026, but there is no public API.
records.bandEvidence: No user, customer or revenue figures are published (checked November 2026); €13.5M raised by February 2024 (TechCrunch) and third-party company profiles put headcount at 11 to 50, unverified.
records.integrationNotes: Gmail, Google Calendar, Slack, GitHub, Linear, Microsoft To Do and email forwarding, all on Basic. An MCP server (May 2026) lets AI assistants manage tasks; there is no public REST API or Zapier connector.
records.calendarSync: Two-way with Google Calendar on Basic: dated tasks become all-day events (30-minute blocks with a time) and edits sync both ways; meetings show in Today. Outlook and iCloud are not supported.
records.dataOut: Whole-account CSV export from Settings (January 2026); neither the January 2026 release note nor the help centre says whether comments or attachments are included. No public REST API; an MCP server can create and update tasks and lists. Data is deleted 30 days after termination.
records.caveat: Pricing was restructured in July 2025 and the free plan is capped at five lists; the vendor publishes no security certifications or user figures.

value.review: A permanent free plan with five lists, then $5 a person annually for unlimited lists, sharing and integrations.

use.review: Wunderlist-style lists with natural-language dates and voice capture; a new user is productive within minutes.

enterprise.review: Team billing and shared lists only: no SSO, admin console, audit log or published certifications.

flex.review: Lists, sublists and rich task pages, but no board, calendar or custom fields, and only an MCP server for extension.

control.review: German company with a named DPO, a DPA on request and Hetzner hosting in Germany, but no certifications.

portability.review: Whole-account CSV export since January 2026, but no public API, and only Microsoft To Do sync as an importer.

commercial.vendor: Superlist GmbH, Germany, built by Christian Reber and the original Wunderlist team. Privately held and remote-first; venture backed by Cherry Ventures and EQT Ventures, with €13.5M raised by February 2024 (TechCrunch).
commercial.yearNote: 2024. Superlist 1.0, released in February 2024 to open the product to new users; beta versions date back to at least January 2023.
commercial.priceNote: Basic, per person per month billed annually ($59 a year); $6 billed monthly. Teams pay the same rate per member.
commercial.freePlanNote: Free for ever with unlimited tasks and notes, but only five private and five shared lists, five people per shared list and 500MB of storage.
commercial.plans: Free; Basic at $6 per person monthly or $59 a year; Super at $25 monthly or $249 a year, adding unlimited AI meeting notes, AI chat and summaries. Legacy Pro ($15 or $149) is closed to new buyers.
commercial.hosting: Hetzner (Germany) is listed for infrastructure and hosting, with DigitalOcean, Cloudflare and Google Cloud as further processors; the policy does not state a data region. No region choice or self-managed edition.
commercial.security: TLS encryption and general technical and organisational measures under GDPR, with a named data protection officer and a DPA on request. No SOC 2 or ISO 27001 claimed. No SSO, SCIM or audit log.
commercial.platforms: Web, macOS, iOS (iPhone and iPad) and Android; Windows users rely on the web app.
commercial.ai: Voice AI capture on Basic; AI meeting notes, AI chat, ‘Make’ content generation and email and Slack summaries on Super. Processors named are Google Gemini, OpenAI and Deepgram; the policy commits only that Google Workspace API data is not used to train general models.

records.name: TeamGantt
records.blurb: Drag-and-drop Gantt scheduling for small teams and builders, priced per account and per project rather than per seat.
summary: TeamGantt is a Gantt chart scheduler that started in 2009 as a tool for a Baltimore roofing contractor, and it has gone back to those roots: its pages now speak mostly to home builders, remodelers and trade contractors, though any small team can use it.

A project is a Gantt chart with groups, tasks, milestones and dependencies, with critical path on every plan; list and calendar views come everywhere, while Kanban, workload, time tracking, portfolios and advanced dependencies start at Business. Builder Edition adds lookahead schedules, material lead times and a Procore sync. Custom workflows are reserved for Builder Edition, and other automation runs through Zapier.

Pricing is by account and project rather than seat. Base is $589 a year for 1 manager, 10 collaborators and 5 projects of up to 150 tasks; Business is $1,140 a year with unlimited people and 5 projects, then $24 a month per project up to 20. Trials need a card.

Data is stored in the United States on AWS with nightly backups; TeamGantt publishes no certifications, no DPA and nothing on how its AI project creation handles data. Leaving is easier: each project exports to CSV, PDF or MS Project, and the REST API covers tasks, time, comments and files.
records.bandEvidence: TeamGantt cites 2M+ users in 120 countries over its life, 20,000+ teams and a staff of 22 (teamgantt.com, about and pricing pages, November 2026).
records.integrationNotes: Procore, Trello, Slack, Dropbox, Basecamp 2 and Zapier, plus an iCal feed and imports from MS Project, Primavera P6 and CSV; a public REST API with token auth and webhooks.
records.calendarSync: One-way iCal feed of your assigned tasks and milestones, or of selected projects, subscribed by URL in Google Calendar, Outlook or Apple Calendar; Google refreshes every few hours.
records.dataOut: Export any project to CSV, PDF or Microsoft Project format on all paid plans. Public REST API (api.teamgantt.com/v1) covering projects, tasks, time blocks, comments, documents, custom fields and webhooks. Imports from MS Project .mpp, Primavera P6 and CSV.
records.caveat: Pricing is now a flat account fee with project caps (pricing page republished in September 2026), not the per-manager seats TeamGantt used to sell, so older comparisons quote the wrong model.

value.review: No per-seat bill, but Base caps at five projects and Business charges $24 a month for each project beyond five.

use.review: Drag-and-drop bars and dependencies on one Gantt screen, and collaborators can only update progress, not reshape the plan.

enterprise.review: SSO only on the quoted Enterprise plan, no published certifications and a simple manager and collaborator model.

flex.review: Gantt, list, calendar and Kanban views with workload and portfolio views; custom workflows only in Builder Edition.

control.review: US-only hosting on AWS, no certifications and a privacy policy that never mentions a DPA or AI.

portability.review: Any project exports to CSV, PDF or MS Project format, and the REST API reaches tasks, time, comments and documents.

sync.note: A one-way iCal feed of assigned tasks and milestones, or chosen projects, for Google Calendar, Outlook or Apple Calendar.

commercial.vendor: TeamGantt. Bootstrapped and privately held, never taken outside equity; headquartered in Baltimore, Maryland, US, with a fully remote team of 22.
commercial.yearNote: 2009. Year TeamGantt was founded and first built; the vendor does not date the first public release separately.
commercial.priceNote: Flat account pricing, not per user: Base is $589 a year (about $49.08 a month) or $59 billed monthly, for 1 manager, 10 collaborators and 5 projects.
commercial.priceDagger: Flat account pricing, not per user: Base is $589 a year (about $49.08 a month) or $59 billed monthly, for 1 manager, 10 collaborators and 5 projects. Shown as $4.91 a person: the cost for a ten-person team.
commercial.freePlanNote: TeamGantt Personal is free for 1 user, 1 project and 40 tasks with basic Gantt features and dependencies; anything shared needs a paid plan.
commercial.plans: Personal free; Base $59 a month or $589 a year; Business from $120 a month or $1,140 a year with 5 projects, plus $24 a month per extra project up to 20; Builder Edition from $199 a month or $1,908 a year; Enterprise by quote.
commercial.hosting: Amazon Web Services; the privacy policy says personal information is stored in the United States. No region choice and no self-managed edition.
commercial.security: SSL in transit, encrypted passwords, uploaded files served only through an authenticated script, two nightly backups. No SOC 2 or ISO 27001 published; SSO only on Enterprise.
commercial.platforms: Web on Mac and PC; iOS and Android apps.
commercial.ai: AI project creation on all paid plans and a free AI Gantt chart maker on the website; the privacy policy names no AI provider and says nothing on training.

records.name: Teamhood
records.blurb: Project and resource planning on boards, lists, Gantt and schedules, aimed at engineering and architecture firms. One paid plan, EU-hosted.
summary: Teamhood is a project planning service from a Lithuanian company that now sells mainly to engineering, architecture and other technical firms running many projects with the same people. Its pitch is resource planning: showing each person’s planned hours across every project so overbooking is visible.

Work is built from configurable item types and fields, shown in list, board, Gantt, schedule, mind map, timesheet and chart views. The Gantt reschedules dependent items, keeps baselines and previews what a change will move; the schedule view becomes a capacity plan when grouped by person. There is no calendar view, no calendar sync and no mobile app.

The current product has one paid plan at $12 (€11) per user per month billed annually, with a three-licence minimum and guests counted as members. There is no free plan, only a one-month trial. Enterprise is quote-only. Customers of the earlier Teamhood Classic keep its separate four-plan structure.

Data sits on Microsoft Azure in the EU; Enterprise can choose Germany or the US, or run dedicated, hybrid or on-premise installations. Teamhood holds no ISO 27001 or SOC 2 of its own. The Chat assistant uses OpenAI with stored responses off. List views export to Excel and CSV and the REST API reads everything, but only while the subscription is paid.
records.bandEvidence: Teamhood’s homepage (read November 2026) claims more than 1,000 companies in 40+ countries, a largest customer of about 3,000 users and 67 G2 reviews.
records.integrationNotes: Packaged connectors are few: SharePoint and OneDrive file links, Microsoft Project XML, Primavera P6 and CSV import, and an MCP server for Claude, ChatGPT, Copilot and Cursor; a full REST API with an OpenAPI document and webhooks is on the standard plan.
records.calendarSync: None documented: no Google or Outlook sync and no iCal feed.
records.dataOut: List views export visible columns to Excel or CSV; timesheets export with cost; Gantt downloads as PDF; a REST API (200 requests a minute per organisation) and webhooks read everything, including per-item history. A lapsed organisation is closed and cannot export until renewed.
records.caveat: Teamhood’s four-plan line-up (Personal, Team, Business, Enterprise) was renamed as recently as 3 December 2025; since then new customers get the rebuilt product on a single paid plan, while the earlier product, now Teamhood Classic, keeps those plans for existing customers. The vendor gives no switch date and no support timeline for Classic.

value.review: No free plan and a three-licence minimum at $12, though API, AI chat and resource planning are all included.

use.review: Configurable item types, fields and roles suit planners, but a new team has setup to do before it works.

enterprise.review: Custom roles, portfolio views and forced two-factor sign-in; SSO and SCIM only on quote-based Enterprise, and no own certification.

flex.review: List, board, Gantt, schedule, mind map, timesheet and chart views with formula fields, templates and rollups, but no calendar.

control.review: EU Azure hosting by default, with Enterprise choices of Germany, US, dedicated, hybrid or on-premise installation.

portability.review: Excel and CSV export from list views and a full REST API, but a lapsed organisation cannot read its own data.

commercial.vendor: UAB Eylean, Vilnius, Lithuania. Privately held; makers of Eylean Board since 2011, with Vidas Vasiliauskas as CEO.
commercial.yearNote: 2020. Approximate: a 2024 vendor blog post says the first Teamhood version went live four years and 100 releases earlier, and a May 2021 press release already describes an upgrade of the platform; Eylean itself dates from 2011.
commercial.priceNote: The single Teamhood plan, per user per month billed annually (€11); $16 (€14) billed monthly, excluding VAT, with a 3-licence minimum and guests counted as licences.
commercial.priceDagger: The single Teamhood plan, per user per month billed annually (€11); $16 (€14) billed monthly, excluding VAT, with a 3-licence minimum and guests counted as licences.
commercial.freePlanNote: No free plan: the first month is a free trial without a card, after which every member, open invite and guest needs a paid licence.
commercial.plans: Teamhood $12 (€11) per user per month billed annually or $16 (€14) monthly, minimum 3 licences; Enterprise is quote-only and adds SSO, SCIM, invoice billing and dedicated, hybrid or on-premise hosting. Existing customers on Teamhood Classic keep its Personal (free), Team, Business and Enterprise plans.
commercial.hosting: Microsoft Azure in the EU with failover to another EU region; Enterprise can pick the EU, Germany or the US, or dedicated, hybrid (database on the customer’s servers) or on-premise hosting with customer-installed updates.
commercial.security: Teamhood states it holds neither ISO 27001 nor SOC 2 (Azure does); TLS in transit, encryption at rest, hourly backups with 7-day point-in-time restore, organisation-wide 2FA on every plan; SSO and SCIM on Enterprise; a DPA from UAB Eylean lists subprocessors.
commercial.platforms: Web only; the vendor states there are no mobile apps.
commercial.ai: In-app Chat on every licence uses OpenAI with stored responses turned off; OpenAI keeps API data up to 30 days for abuse checks and does not train on it. An MCP server lets external assistants read and change data. Admins can turn Chat off but cannot block MCP organisation-wide.

records.name: Toodledo
records.blurb: Dense, long-running task manager with folders, contexts, goals and custom columns, plus notes, outlines, lists, habits and a per-task timer.
summary: Toodledo is one of the oldest web task managers, built for people who want to slice a long task list by folder, context, goal, priority and length. It suits GTD-style planners who are comfortable with a spreadsheet-like screen.

Tasks carry a long list of fields and can be sorted, filtered and saved as searches, with a Hotlist for what matters now. Beside tasks sit notes, hierarchical outlines, custom lists, habit tracking, a scheduler, an in-app calendar and a per-task timer. There is no board, timeline or rule automation, and collaboration is limited to sharing folders with named collaborators.

The free plan stops at 10 folders, 30 items per list and a week of history, and leaves out subtasks and calendar sync. Standard at $3.99 a month billed annually removes most limits; Plus at $5.99 adds the scheduler, file uploads and up to 5 collaborators. Business is sold by quote.

Data sits on US servers at Rackspace with nightly off-site backups; the vendor says only some data is encrypted at rest and publishes no certifications or AI features. Leaving is easy: a backup tool, several export formats and a free API cover the data.
records.bandEvidence: The press page claims over a million users and more than 100 million tasks managed (undated, checked November 2026); no revenue, staff or recent growth figures are published.
records.integrationNotes: The vendor claims more than 50 third-party apps and tools, mostly sync clients for iOS, Android and desktop, plus IFTTT, a Google Calendar widget and email-to-task on Plus; a free API v3 covers tasks, notes, outlines and lists, with no webhooks documented.
records.calendarSync: One-way Live iCal Link to Google Calendar, Apple Calendar and others on Standard and above, placing tasks by start, due and length; Google refreshes it about once a day. A one-off ICS download is also offered.
records.dataOut: Backup/Restore tool plus exports including iCal; imports from CSV, JSON, XML, text and iCal, with guides for Outlook and Remember The Milk. The free API v3 covers tasks, notes, outlines, lists, folders, contexts, goals and locations.
records.caveat: The privacy policy has not been updated since October 2018 and still refers to the EU-US Privacy Shield, which the EU Court of Justice struck down in 2020.

value.review: A free plan for light use, then $3.99 a month for Standard, though subtasks and calendar sync start there.

use.review: Many columns, contexts and settings suit dedicated list-makers but take newcomers a while to set up.

enterprise.review: Per-collaborator folder permissions and a quote-only Business plan, but no SSO, audit log or certifications are documented.

flex.review: Custom columns, outlines, lists, notes, habits, goals and a calendar, but no board, timeline or automation rules.

control.review: US servers at Rackspace, only some data encrypted at rest, no certifications, and a 2018 privacy policy.

portability.review: Backup and restore, exports and imports in CSV, XML, JSON and iCal, and a free API covering tasks and notes.

tt.note: A per-task timer column records actual time against estimated length and can run several timers, but there are no time reports or timesheets.

sync.note: A Live iCal Link sends dated tasks one way to Google, Apple and other calendars (Standard and above), and Google refreshes it about once a day.

commercial.vendor: Toodledo, Inc. Privately held; its terms give a New York, USA mailing address and California governing law, and no owners or executives are named.
commercial.yearNote: 2004. The service dates from 2004, per the vendor’s copyright line, which starts in 2004, and its press page’s “over the last 22 years”.
commercial.priceNote: Standard, per person per month billed annually; $4.99 billed monthly. Plus is $5.99 billed annually or $7.99 monthly; Business is quote-only.
commercial.freePlanNote: Free has unlimited tasks with notes, repeats, search and sync, but caps folders at 10, lists and outlines at 30 items, habits at 5 and history at one week, and leaves out subtasks and calendar sync.
commercial.plans: Free; Standard at $3.99 a month billed annually or $4.99 monthly; Plus at $5.99 billed annually or $7.99 monthly with 5 collaborators and 10 GB of files; Business by quote.
commercial.hosting: Servers in the United States, with Rackspace named as hosting provider; redundant storage and nightly off-site backups. No region choice or self-managed edition.
commercial.security: SSL on all connections and two-step authentication; the vendor says some data is encrypted at rest and it is working towards all of it. No certifications, SSO, SCIM or audit log are published. The privacy policy, last updated October 2018, still cites Privacy Shield for EU transfers.
commercial.platforms: Web, iOS and Android apps, desktop apps, and dozens of third-party clients listed in the vendor’s directory.
commercial.ai: None.

records.name: Tweek
records.blurb: A minimal weekly planner that lays out to-dos like a paper diary, one column per day, with shared calendars and optional calendar sync.
summary: Tweek is a weekly planner that looks like a paper diary: seven columns, one per day, with tasks written straight into them. It suits individuals, couples and families who want a shared week rather than a project tool.

Unfinished tasks roll over to the next day, ‘Someday’ columns hold undated items, and colour carries most of the organisation. Calendars can be shared with anyone or published as a web page. Month and day views, recurring tasks, reminders and subtasks are there; boards, projects, custom fields and time tracking are not.

The free plan is generous for one calendar. Premium costs $49.99 a year or $5.99 a month and adds calendar sync, reminders, recurring tasks, subtasks, attachments and export, while Family at $89.99 a year covers five people.

The vendor is Scada SIA in Riga, and data lives in Google Cloud Firestore with encryption at rest; the processor list places Google Cloud and DigitalOcean in the USA, and no certification is stated. An AI assistant described in the terms uses Anthropic’s Claude, with OpenAI for voice, and the terms say neither the providers nor Tweek train on your tasks. Export to CSV, XML, TXT or ICS and an open REST API make leaving easy.
records.bandEvidence: The vendor cites 6,500+ App Store ratings at 4.8 and 3,600+ Google Play ratings at 4.4 (November 2026) and 1,200 Product Hunt followers; no user or revenue figures are published.
records.integrationNotes: Google Calendar, Outlook Calendar, Google Tasks, Linear, .ics subscriptions, and Apple Calendar and Reminders in the Apple apps, plus official ChatGPT and Claude apps. A public REST API and an MCP server work on every plan (15k reads and 3k writes a month free, 150k/30k on Premium).
records.calendarSync: Premium: Google Calendar events sync both ways for title, description, date and time (deletions and completion one way, from Google); Tweek tasks are not sent to Google. Outlook Calendar imports events; the help centre still calls it one-way, but the October 2026 changelog says time changes to synced events now reach Outlook. .ics feeds import one way; Apple Calendar and Reminders in the Apple apps; Google Tasks two-way since October 2026.
records.dataOut: Web-only export per calendar and date range to XML, TXT, CSV or ICS (Premium). REST API and MCP server for reading and writing tasks and calendars on every plan, with monthly request quotas.
records.caveat: Tweek tasks never reach Google or Outlook calendars; only synced events can be edited from Tweek (Google fully, Outlook times since October 2026), so it does not work as a time-blocking tool.

value.review: A usable free plan with sharing, then $49.99 a year for one person or $89.99 for a family of five.

use.review: A week laid out like a paper diary: type into a day, drag to another; there is almost nothing to learn.

enterprise.review: No admin console, SSO, audit log or certifications; team use means sharing a calendar link.

flex.review: Week, month and day views, Someday lists, colour rules and an API, but no boards, custom fields or projects.

control.review: A Latvian GDPR controller whose Google Cloud and DigitalOcean processors are listed in the USA, with no certifications.

portability.review: Per-calendar export to CSV, XML, TXT or ICS on the web, and a REST API even on the free plan.

sync.note: Google event titles, notes, dates and times sync both ways, but Tweek tasks are never sent to a calendar; Outlook imports events, and since October 2026 time changes go back. Premium only.

commercial.vendor: Scada SIA, Riga, Latvia (EU). Privately held; the App Store lists the copyright as Scada Inc.
commercial.yearNote: 2020. Product Hunt launch in 2020 (ranked second of the day on 2 September 2020); Tweek 2.0 followed in June 2022.
commercial.priceNote: Premium Individual, per person per month billed annually ($49.99 a year); $5.99 billed monthly. Family covers five people for $89.99 a year or $9.99 a month.
commercial.freePlanNote: Free for ever with one active calendar, two custom colours, notes on tasks and sharing; calendar sync, subtasks, attachments, reminders, recurring tasks and export need Premium.
commercial.plans: Free; Individual $5.99 a month or $49.99 a year (14-day trial on annual only); Family for up to five people at $9.99 a month or $89.99 a year.
commercial.hosting: Google Cloud Firestore, replicated across at least three zones in a regional database. The privacy policy lists Google Cloud (cloud services) and DigitalOcean (hosting) as US sub-processors; the Firestore region itself is not named. No region choice and no self-managed edition.
commercial.security: Encryption at rest with Google-managed keys and TLS in transit, per the vendor’s security page. GDPR controller in Latvia. No SOC 2 or ISO 27001 claimed. No SSO, SCIM or audit log.
commercial.platforms: Web, iOS and iPadOS, Android, and a native Mac app (November 2026).
commercial.ai: An in-app assistant that answers questions and creates, changes or deletes tasks by text or voice, run on Anthropic’s Claude with OpenAI transcription and Google Cloud (EU) speech. The terms give every plan, free included, its own request limit; the assistant is not yet listed on the pricing, features or changelog pages (November 2026). ChatGPT and Claude apps and the MCP server work on both plans. The terms state neither Tweek nor its providers train AI models on your tasks, messages or voice.

records.name: Workflowy
records.blurb: An infinitely nested bullet outline used for notes and to-dos, with any branch viewable as a board, table or dated calendar entry.
summary: Workflowy is a browser outliner in which everything, from a shopping list to a book draft, is a bullet that can hold more bullets. It suits individuals who think in nested lists and want notes and to-dos in one place.

You zoom into any bullet to make it the page, tag and mirror items across the outline, and turn any branch into a board, table, to-do list or document. A daily calendar note collects dated items, and since 2026 a timeline and read-only Google Calendar import sit beside it. There is no time tracking, dependency chart or assignee field; @mentions do that job.

The free plan has every feature but caps new content at 100 nodes a month, a limit a daily planner will meet quickly since each bullet counts. Pro costs $6.99 a month on an annual plan or $8.99 monthly, and Teams costs the same per user.

Data is stored on AWS in Northern Virginia, and the privacy policy (February 2026) names no certifications for Workflowy itself. AI chat, AI nodes and actions on Pro send content to OpenAI and Anthropic, which the AI terms say may not train on it. Exports to OPML and Markdown, Dropbox backup and a public API make leaving straightforward.
records.bandEvidence: No user, revenue or staff figures are published (checked November 2026); the homepage cites ‘over 14 years’ of service and Wikipedia describes a cult following.
records.integrationNotes: Google Calendar (read-only), Readwise, Kindle highlights, a web clipper, email-to-Workflowy, Dropbox backup and Zapier (inbound recipes), plus a desktop MCP server. A public JSON REST API with API keys covers create, update, move, complete and export-all; no webhooks are documented.
records.calendarSync: One-way, read-only import of Google Calendar events into the Workflowy Calendar, refreshed hourly for the next 35 days, on all plans. No Outlook or iCloud, and no feed out.
records.dataOut: Any bullet or the whole account exports as plain text, formatted text, Markdown or OPML; tables export to HTML, Markdown or TSV; Pro and Teams add automatic Dropbox backup. Public REST API with an export-all endpoint and a desktop MCP server.
records.caveat: The free plan’s 100-nodes-a-month cap is a soft limit enforced by prompts, so heavy free use is possible but nagged.

value.review: Every feature is free up to 100 new nodes a month, then $6.99 a person annually, with free Pro for academics.

use.review: One outline of bullets that you indent and zoom into; a new user is productive in minutes.

enterprise.review: Team billing, node-level sharing permissions and MFA, but no SSO, admin console, audit log or certifications.

flex.review: Boards, tables, calendar, timeline, mirrors, templates, AI nodes and an API, all built on one outline without custom fields.

control.review: Data on AWS in Northern Virginia with no region choice and no certifications of its own, under a GDPR-aware policy.

portability.review: Whole-account export to OPML, Markdown or plain text, Dropbox backups and a public API with export-all.

gantt.note: Timeline (May 2026) shows the next 30 days and 12 months for drag-to-date scheduling, without dependencies or bars.

calendar.note: Calendar is a daily note per date with dated items gathered in, not a month grid of tasks.

sync.note: One-way: Google Calendar events are imported hourly, read-only, for the next 35 days; nothing is written back.

commercial.vendor: FunRoutine, Inc., a privately held US company with its official address in Centennial, Colorado.
commercial.yearNote: 2010. Public release of the web outliner in August 2010, created by Mike Turitzin and Jesse Patel after a Y Combinator startup camp.
commercial.priceNote: Pro, per person per month billed annually; $8.99 billed monthly. Teams pay $6.99 per user per month billed annually.
commercial.freePlanNote: Free for ever with every feature, but capped at 100 new nodes a month and 100MB of uploads; past the cap you can still add nodes but are prompted to subscribe.
commercial.plans: Basic free; Pro $6.99 a month billed annually or $8.99 monthly; Teams $6.99 per user a month billed annually with Dropbox backup and setup help. Free Pro for university staff and students, 50% off for non-profits.
commercial.hosting: Amazon Web Services in US Northern Virginia, per the privacy policy (updated February 2026); Google Workspace for business operations. No region choice and no self-managed edition.
commercial.security: Emailed one-time codes or passwords, plus optional multi-factor authentication. The policy cites AWS’s ISO 27001/27017/27018 certifications but claims none for Workflowy. No SSO, SCIM or audit log.
commercial.platforms: Web, macOS, Windows and Linux desktop apps, iOS and iPadOS, Android, and a browser web clipper.
commercial.ai: Chat with your notes, AI Nodes and AI Actions for Pro subscribers who enable AI, processed by OpenAI and Anthropic. The AI terms (March 2025) state sub-processors are not authorised to use data for model training.

records.name: Workzone
records.blurb: Project management for marketing, creative and operations teams, with Gantt, boards, intake requests, proofing and bundled human training.
summary: Workzone is an American project management service sold to marketing, creative and operations teams in universities, healthcare, banks and non-profits. Its distinguishing offer is people: onboarding, unlimited training and phone support are included in the price.

Projects are planned as task lists and Gantt charts with dependencies, alongside simpler card boards, a cross-workspace calendar, a personal to-do list and portfolio status reports. Intake request forms, document proofing with markups and approvals, timesheets and workload reports serve agency-style work. Custom fields and critical path arrive only on Enterprise.

There is no free plan and every tier is billed annually. Starter at $8 per user per month suits up to 25 users; Team at $20, with a five-user minimum, is where time tracking, intake and proofing begin. Enterprise is quote-based and charges only for core users, with five free collaborators each.

Data is processed in the United States with no region choice; Workzone states SOC 2 Type II and offers a HIPAA BAA on Enterprise. Its AI runs on an open-weight model inside its own environment and is not trained on customer data. Getting data out is the weak point: the API is a paid Enterprise feature.
records.bandEvidence: Workzone publishes no customer or user count; its about page (read November 2026) cites 2.7 million completed projects and a seven-year average customer relationship.
records.integrationNotes: Native Microsoft Teams, Slack, Google Drive and OneDrive, Outlook import and Microsoft Project export; Zapier, Power BI and Tableau (via OData) and the OAuth REST API are Enterprise or paid add-ons.
records.calendarSync: One-way webcal subscription per user, pushing the to-do list (7 days back, 30 ahead) to Outlook, Google or other calendars as all-day events; Outlook events can be imported; Google Calendar and Outlook sync otherwise via Zapier on Enterprise.
records.dataOut: Single projects export to a Microsoft Project file; OData feeds for Power BI and Tableau and an OAuth 2 REST API are Enterprise or paid add-ons. No bulk CSV or JSON export is documented.
records.caveat: Workzone’s API, Zapier connection and SSO are held to Enterprise, and every plan is billed a year at a time, so a team should confirm how it will get its data out before committing.

value.review: No free plan and annual billing only; $8 Starter stops at 25 users, Team is $20 with five seats minimum.

use.review: The vendor plans three to four weeks of human-led onboarding before a team goes live.

enterprise.review: SOC 2 Type II, HIPAA BAA, SAML SSO, enforced MFA and activity logs, with SSO and API held to Enterprise.

flex.review: List, Gantt, Kanban, calendar and portfolio views with intake forms, proofing and dashboards; custom fields only on Enterprise.

control.review: SOC 2 Type II and an in-house AI model, but US-only processing with no region choice.

portability.review: Projects export one at a time to Microsoft Project; the API is an Enterprise add-on and no bulk export is documented.

sync.note: One-way webcal subscription of a user’s to-do list (previous 7 and next 30 days) into Outlook or Google; Zapier sync is Enterprise only.

commercial.vendor: WorkZone, LLC, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, USA (the privacy policy also gives a Blue Bell, Pennsylvania address). Privately owned per a 2017 vendor press release; founded by Rick and Allan in the early 2000s, with no parent company or investors named.
commercial.yearNote: 2002. Service in use since 2002, per a June 2017 vendor press release (“serving diverse industries and projects since 2002”); the about page says only that the company was founded in the early 2000s.
commercial.priceNote: Starter, per user per month, billed annually only (no monthly option), for 1 to 25 users; Team is $20 with a 5-user minimum.
commercial.priceDagger: Starter, per user per month, billed annually only (no monthly option), for 1 to 25 users; Team is $20 with a 5-user minimum.
commercial.freePlanNote: No free plan: a 14-day trial without a card, then annual billing on every tier.
commercial.plans: Starter $8 per user per month billed annually (1 to 25 users, 100 active projects, 3 workspaces); Team $20 (5 users or more) adds time and expense tracking, intake forms, proofing and workload planning; Enterprise is quote-only, charges only core users and adds API, Zapier, SSO, custom fields and HIPAA.
commercial.hosting: Primary processing in the United States per the DPA (updated February 2026), with EU Standard Contractual Clauses for EEA transfers; the hosting provider, region and subprocessors are not named, and there is no residency choice or self-managed edition.
commercial.security: SOC 2 Type II; HIPAA support with a BAA on Enterprise; HECVAT and VPAT in the trust centre; encryption in transit and at rest for sensitive stores, hourly off-site backups; activity logs on every plan; SAML SSO on Enterprise; MFA optional or enforced.
commercial.platforms: Web, with a mobile-optimised browser interface for iOS and Android; no native apps.
commercial.ai: AI features run on an open-weight model hosted inside Workzone’s own firewalled environment, with no third-party AI providers, no training on customer data and per-user or per-company switches.

records.name: Zenkit Projects
records.blurb: Database-style project tool with table, Kanban, list, calendar, Gantt, mind map and wiki views over the same items. Hosted in Germany.
summary: Zenkit Projects is a German work-management service in which every project is a list of items with typed fields that can be shown in eight ways. It suits small and mid-sized teams who want spreadsheet structure and project views in one place, with data kept in Germany.

The same list can appear as a table, Kanban board, plain list, calendar, Gantt chart, mind map, hierarchy or wiki. The Gantt supports dependencies and milestones; critical path, lag and other dependency types need Business. Automations, dashboards and portfolios sit on top. There is no time tracking.

There is no free plan, only a 14-day trial. Plus at $8 per seat (annual) caps the organisation at 10 users and 6 GB; Team at $12 removes the user cap and adds the iCal feed; Business at $21 adds the API, SAML SSO, SCIM and activity auditing. Quotas on items, comments and automation runs apply to every tier.

All data and backups are on AWS in Frankfurt, encrypted at rest, with a GDPR DPA on request; Zenkit cites AWS’s ISO 27001 rather than its own. AI features, priced on request, run in the EU and are not trained on customer data. Lists export to CSV or JSON, so leaving is practical list by list.
records.bandEvidence: The vendor publishes no current Zenkit user count (about page, read November 2026, cites only 5 million users for Axonic’s earlier products); the English blog’s last post is dated December 2024, while the German blog posts monthly through October 2026.
records.integrationNotes: Built-in Google Calendar sync, Trello, Asana, Excel and Access importers and file-storage connectors; most other links (Slack, Teams, Toggl, Clockify) run through Zapier or Integrately. A REST API is on Business and above.
records.calendarSync: Two-way Google Calendar sync per list, including creating and deleting entries (recurring tasks Zenkit to Google only); Outlook and Apple Calendar only through a one-way iCalendar subscription, which the pricing table places on Team and above.
records.dataOut: Per-list export to CSV or JSON, files as a ZIP, and printing; importers for Trello, Asana, CSV, Excel, Google Sheets and Microsoft Access; REST API on Business and above. After a lapsed trial the organisation is usually limited to export before deletion.
records.caveat: The product is still sold and maintained: the pricing, terms and security pages were revised in October and November 2026, the German blog posts monthly and a Zenkit Processes workflow module appeared in late 2025. But the English blog has been silent since December 2024, no dated public changelog is readable, and the help centre still documents a Free plan the pricing page no longer offers, so confirm plan terms in the trial.

value.review: No free plan; $8 Plus stops at 10 users, and API and SSO need Business at $21 a seat.

use.review: Lists switch between eight views without setup, but fields, list types and hierarchies take time to learn.

enterprise.review: SAML SSO, SCIM, activity audit and central user management on Business; no certification held by Zenkit itself.

flex.review: Table, Kanban, list, calendar, Gantt, mind map, hierarchy and wiki views with custom fields, automations, dashboards and forms.

control.review: Every account sits on AWS in Frankfurt with an Article 28 DPA, but there is no region choice or own certification.

portability.review: Lists export to CSV or JSON with files as ZIP, Trello and Asana importers, but the API needs Business.

commercial.vendor: Axonic GmbH, Karlsruhe, Germany (Amtsgericht Mannheim HRB 110424); privately held, managed by Martin Welker. Axonic also makes Zenkit To Do, Hypernotes, Zenforms and Zenchat.
commercial.yearNote: 2016. Public release of Zenkit in October 2016, per the vendor’s about page; work began at Axonic in 2014.
commercial.priceNote: Plus, per seat per month billed annually ($9 monthly, also €8 and €9), excluding VAT, capped at 10 users; Team at $12 ($14) is the first plan without a user cap.
commercial.priceDagger: Plus, per seat per month billed annually ($9 monthly, also €8 and €9), excluding VAT, capped at 10 users; Team at $12 ($14) is the first plan without a user cap.
commercial.freePlanNote: No free plan on the current pricing page: a 14-day trial, after which an unpaid organisation is usually limited to data export and later deleted.
commercial.plans: Plus $8 per seat per month billed annually ($9 monthly), up to 10 users; Team $12 ($14); Business $21 ($25) with API, SSO, SCIM and activity audit; Enterprise quote-only. Prices cover Zenkit Projects only; Zenkit AI and Zenkit Flow are on request.
commercial.hosting: AWS Frankfurt (RDS and S3, contracted through AWS Luxembourg), with encrypted daily backups in a separate Frankfurt data centre. No region choice and no on-premise edition documented.
commercial.security: TLS 1.2+, AES-256 at rest, Argon2 password hashing, app-based 2FA on all plans; SAML SSO, SCIM, activity auditing and central user management on Business; certifications cited are AWS’s (ISO 27001, SSAE 16), not Zenkit’s; GDPR DPA available by email.
commercial.platforms: Web, iOS, Android, and desktop apps for Windows, macOS and Linux.
commercial.ai: Zenkit AI is sold on request; the vendor says AI runs in the EU, calls models statelessly, does not store inputs or train on customer data, and asks for approval before modifying actions.

records.name: Amazing Marvin
records.blurb: A single-user task manager and day planner built from switchable ‘strategies’, aimed at procrastinators and people with ADHD.
summary: Amazing Marvin is a personal task manager and day planner that a Swiss micro-company has run since 2017. It is sold to individuals who struggle with procrastination or ADHD and want to tune the tool to how their own head works.

Every feature is a ‘strategy’ you switch on or off: Kanban boards, a calendar with time blocking, time tracking, habits, goals, a task jar, reward points and procrastination prompts. The result can be a plain checklist or a dense personal system. There are no Gantt charts and no team workspaces; the only AI feature is a braindump sorter in the mobile apps.

There is one plan, Marvin Pro, at $12 a month or $96 a year, with a 14-day trial and no free tier. Students get half price and the vendor offers pay-what-you-can on request, which is unusual. The mobile apps were rebuilt in September 2026.

The privacy policy, last updated in January 2020, names Google App Engine and IBM Cloudant for storage, with US transfers; there are no certifications. Cloud sync can be turned off so data stays in the browser or desktop app. Backups export everything as JSON, and a documented API with webhooks and full database access makes leaving realistic.
records.bandEvidence: The homepage claims ‘5K+ happy users’ and the About page names three staff (both checked November 2026); no revenue or customer figures are published.
records.integrationNotes: Calendar sync (Google, iCloud, Yahoo, CalDAV, Outlook in beta), Zapier, email-to-Marvin, a browser extension, Siri and Alexa; importers for Todoist, TickTick, Things, OmniFocus and CSV. A REST API with webhooks and direct database access is documented.
records.calendarSync: Two-way sync with Google, iCloud, Yahoo and CalDAV calendars on the single plan; Outlook and Exchange sync is in beta, and public ICS feeds can be imported read-only.
records.dataOut: Backup of all data (tasks, projects, labels, time blocks, settings, notebooks, habits) as compressed or plain JSON; automatic backups in the desktop app; REST API, webhooks and direct CouchDB access. Projects can be copied out as text; no CSV export.
records.caveat: The privacy policy has not been updated since January 2020, so its hosting and transfer statements may not reflect current practice, and it says nothing about the AI braindump added to the mobile apps in September 2026.

value.review: No free plan, and $8 a month annually or $12 monthly is high for a one-person tool, though everything is included.

use.review: Over 100 features and 300 settings switched on one by one; productive quickly only once you choose a workflow.

enterprise.review: A single-user tool by design: no admin console, no SSO, and only light task sharing and comments.

flex.review: Lists, Kanban, calendar, smart lists, custom screens and dozens of toggled strategies, plus API and webhooks; no custom fields.

control.review: No certifications and a 2020 privacy policy naming US clouds, but cloud sync can be switched off to keep data local.

portability.review: Full JSON backup of tasks, projects and settings, a read-write API and many importers; no CSV export.

commercial.vendor: Amazing GmbH, a Swiss company founded and run by Christina Willner. Privately held; the About page lists a team of three.
commercial.yearNote: 2017. Public launch of the app, as the vendor’s About page records it (work on it began in 2014).
commercial.priceNote: Marvin Pro, per person per month billed annually ($96 a year); $12 billed monthly. 50% student discount and ‘pay what you can’ on request.
commercial.freePlanNote: No free plan: a 14-day trial without a card, after which data is kept but tasks cannot be added or completed until you subscribe.
commercial.plans: One plan, Marvin Pro: $12 a month billed monthly or $96 a year ($8 a month) billed annually, with every feature included.
commercial.hosting: Account data on Google App Engine and task data on IBM Cloudant, with transfers to the USA per the privacy policy (last updated 19 January 2020). No region choice; cloud sync can be disabled to keep data on the device only.
commercial.security: Account data encrypted in transit and at rest, task data in transit (the help centre makes no at-rest claim for tasks), and optional two-factor authentication. No SOC 2 or ISO 27001 claimed. No SSO, SCIM or audit log.
commercial.platforms: Web, macOS, Windows, Linux, iOS, Android, Apple Watch and a browser extension.
commercial.ai: AI Braindump in the iOS and Android apps rebuilt in September 2026: typed or spoken text is sorted into tasks and projects, not yet on the web. The vendor names no AI provider and the January 2020 privacy policy does not mention AI or training.

records.name: Todoi
records.blurb: A small, free task manager that opens ready to use in a browser tab: each project seen as a list, a board and a calendar, with no account.
summary: Todoi is a young, deliberately small task manager, on todoi.com since November 2025. It suits one person planning a day or a small piece of work who wants to start typing without signing up for anything. The app is closed source, but its developer releases core features as open-source projects.

Each project is shown three ways over the same items: a list, a board whose columns are the project’s lists, and a month calendar that undated items can be dragged onto. Items carry subitems, tags, due dates, priorities and notes, with search, filters, sorting and keyboard shortcuts for the views. Edits apply at once because nothing goes to a server, and there is nothing to set up. Time tracking, Gantt and collaboration are not part of it; the app is young and still being developed, with product notes published through August 2026.
It is free: there is no paid plan, no trial and no account, and no caps are published.

Tasks never leave the browser. The workspace is held in the tab’s session storage, so the vendor has no copy of it and there is no assistant reading it. The other side of that choice, which the vendor calls deliberate, is that closing the tab clears the workspace; there is no sync, export or API.
records.bandEvidence: No user, customer or revenue figures are published (checked November 2026); the contact page names one lead developer, and the app is free with no paid plan.
records.integrationNotes: None: no connectors, importers, API or webhooks.
records.calendarSync: None. The calendar is a month view inside the app; nothing is exchanged with Google, Outlook or an iCal feed.
records.dataOut: No export, API or importer. The workspace exists only in the tab’s session storage and is cleared when the tab closes, so text leaves by copy and paste; the vendor’s terms say to keep your own copy of anything you need tomorrow.
records.caveat: The workspace lasts only as long as the browser tab: there is no account, sync or backup, so it works as a scratch space rather than a record. Todoi is built by this directory’s maintainer, which is the qualification behind the confidence value.

value.review: Entirely free with nothing held back and no sign-up; the feature set is small and work does not outlast the tab.

use.review: Opens on an empty project with no sign-up; three plain views, a guided demo and almost nothing to learn, though work must be kept elsewhere.

enterprise.review: A single-user tool by design: no accounts, sharing, admin controls or certifications.

flex.review: List, board and month calendar over the same items, with tags, priorities, filters and sorting; no custom fields, automation or API.

control.review: Tasks stay in your own browser and are never sent to a server or an AI; no certifications, and Google Analytics counts page visits, by default outside Europe.

portability.review: No export, importer or API; nothing is held by the vendor, so leaving means copying out what is in the tab.

commercial.vendor: Todoi; the contact page names Flo Zuallaert as lead developer and gives no company or country. The same developer maintains this directory. The app is closed source; core features are released as open-source projects, such as minimal-to-do (MIT), which Todoi extends.
commercial.yearNote: 2025. todoi.com went live on 21 November 2025, per the vendor’s launch note; the current terms and privacy pages are versioned web-1.0, effective August 2026.
commercial.priceNote: No paid tier: the whole app is free, with no account, trial or seat count.
commercial.freePlanNote: Every feature is free with no sign-up and no published caps; the workspace is kept only for the life of the browser tab.
commercial.plans: One free web app; no paid plans are published.
commercial.hosting: None for task data: the workspace sits in the browser tab’s session storage and is never sent to a server, so there is no region to choose. Once loaded, the app keeps working offline until the page is reloaded.
commercial.security: No account, so no password, SSO, SCIM or audit log. Task data is not held on a server; it is as protected as the device and browser it sits in. Google Analytics counts page visits and loads only after consent in Europe. No SOC 2 or ISO 27001 claimed.
commercial.platforms: Web only; no native apps.
commercial.ai: None. The vendor states that nothing you write is read, summarised, sent anywhere for processing or used for model training.
